title: Show HN: Vela, a New Linux Desktop Environment
author: BrandoDev_it
body:
Hi, take a look at this.
I didn't like KDE nor KDE Themes, so I made Vela, a new stacking desktop environment, and even though this is not very inspired in terms of aesthetic, this is not the point of Vela (not yet).
Point of Vela is mostly architecture: Vulkan 1.4 only, no OpenGL fallback; based on wlroots, but has a custom renderer.
GPL3 license.
Vela is currently at 0.1.0 beta after one month of Alpha testing. Tested and working both on AMD and Nvidia.
Requirements: a GPU and driver with Vulkan 1.4 support.
I’m looking for people to try it on their hardware and report issues, and for contributors. Thankscode: https://github.com/vela-desktop/vela

title: Show HN: BBRouter – Ben Eater's 8-bit computer, simulated on 3D breadboards
author: creack
body: Hi HN,I kept wiring Ben Eater's 8-bit computer wrong, so I built a realistic virtual breadboard editor.Some of the nice features are side-by-side diff, scope, schematics auto-sync, auto-router (BBRouter stands for breadboard router), and my favorites: upload from the real Arduino IDE and connect to your AI with MCP, let Claude & co build it or help you troubleshoot.The link is the SAP-1 running. You can orbit it, probe a hole with the scope, slow the clock down, play with the virtual displays for debugging, then you can actually build it following the step-by-step instructions.A side-goal is to create a community, there are quite a lot of simulators out there but mostly offline / too abstract to realistically use it for a real build. I also never found one that had a decent UI/UX and worked well on mobile or with a trackpad.Happy to answer anything, and tell me what breaks.p.s. Maker plan is $7/month; code HACKERNEWS makes the first month free and then $5/month for as long as you keep it.

title: Show HN: Fix 1.0 – Ruby tests written as RFC 2119 specifications
author: cyrilllllll
body:
Fixrb 
Blog 
Code 
Guide 
Fix 1.0 is here
October 31, 2026 · Cyril Kato
Fix 1.0 is out. Fix is a testing framework for Ruby in which a test suite is a specification: a document that says what a subject MUST , SHOULD or MAY do, in the words of RFC 2119 , and nothing about how the subject is made. I started it in Osaka in 2014 and have reworked it many times since; this is the first version I consider finished.
If it quacks like a duck
Ruby knows a duck by what it does: that is duck typing . A specification of Fix does the same: it names no class, and the test, at the end of the file, picks the subject. Here, a duck and a rubber duck, against one specification:
require "fix" 
Fix :Duck do 
 on :quack do 
 it MUST eq "Quack!" 
 end 
on :swim do 
 it SHOULD eq "Splash!" 
 end 
on :fly do 
 it MAY be_true
 end 
 end 
class Duck 
 def quack = "Quack!" 
 def swim = "Splash!" 
 def fly = true 
 end 
class RubberDuck 
 def quack = "Quack!" 
 def swim = "Splash!" 
 end 
exit([
 Fix [ :Duck ].test { Duck .new },
 Fix [ :Duck ].test { RubberDuck .new }
].all?)
ruby duck_fix.rb 
 duck_fix.rb:5: Success: expected "Quack!" to eq "Quack!"
duck_fix.rb:9: Success: expected "Splash!" to eq "Splash!"
duck_fix.rb:13: Success: expected true to be true
duck_fix.rb:5: Success: expected "Quack!" to eq "Quack!"
duck_fix.rb:9: Success: expected "Splash!" to eq "Splash!"
duck_fix.rb:13: Info: NoMethodError: undefined method 'fly' for an instance of RubberDuck 
 The rubber duck cannot fly, but flying was only a MAY: its line is an info, and both ducks meet the specification. Three levels tell what is required, what is recommended and what is optional, and the lines say exactly what happened, one per expectation; the status of the process says whether the whole is met. The same specification can test a class of yours, a library you depend on, or the next version of either.
What 1.0 brings
A specification is built once, when the file is loaded, and kept as data. Anything wrong in it raises before a test runs.
Each context runs in a child process: what a subject does to a global, a constant or ENV stays in its context, and the order of the contexts cannot change a result.
The matchers are those of Matchi , where the expected value makes the comparison, so that the object under test cannot vouch for itself.
test writes one line per expectation and returns whether the specification is met; run gives the results as data; match? makes a specification a matcher, so that one may require another with fix(:Name) .
About three hundred lines of code, with tests written by hand at full coverage, on Ruby 3.3, 3.4 and 4.0, resting on four small gems, matchi , spectus , aw and defi , each short enough to read before you trust it.
Around it: fix-command runs the files of a project, fix-its adds the word its , and matchi-fix brings a specification to any other test framework.
Try it
gem install fix-command 
 Then the guide : a first specification, the language, the matchers one by one, the command, and what changes when you come from RSpec. Every example on its pages is run before they are published. The README is the reference. Fix needs Ruby 3.3 or later and fork(2) .
Write a specification for something you have, and see what it says. That is what Fix is for.
Filed under framework and release. All posts 
Fixrb is made by Cyril Kato and sponsored by Sashité . The gems and this site are released under the MIT license.

title: Show HN: Gitmsg – A messenger where every message is a Git commit
author: eugenepavlov
body:
Connecting… Some things should exist just for the fun of it.
 We turned GitHub into a messenger. Chats are repositories. Messages are commits. “I never said that” now comes with a git log . Not because the world needed another chat app — because we wanted to see if it would work. 
 No pitch deck. No grand plan to reinvent human connection. Just a weird idea, a familiar interface, and the unreasonable satisfaction of making them fit. Software can still be a playground. 
 Bring your GitHub account. Invite a friend. Send a photo, leave a voice note, react to something stupid. No fake conversations, no bot pretending to be your friend. Real people. Real messages. A little Git underneath. 
 No magic privacy claims, either. GitHub can read standard messages; public channels are public. Browser encryption is optional, and your keys are yours to keep. Deleting a message hides it from the chat — Git still remembers. 
 Not everything needs to become the next big thing. Sometimes “holy shit, it works” is enough.

title: Show HN: Othismo, a Runtime for Sandboxed Objects
author: mamidon
body:
Othismo is a runtime which has a bunch of sandboxed WASM modules talking to each other + the host environment. It's actually hosting its own website right now at othismo.com.This is a project that's been percolating in my head for a while, as a vague desire to make a "better" runtime for software development. But it was never particularly clear for me what that would _actually_ look like. In the last month or so, I felt a bit inspired to ask what such a runtime might look like for agentic development.My hypothesis is that we really can't review 10k+ SLoC pull requests consistently and really understand them. But if we try to have a higher level view of things, we still can't be confident the agent(s) haven't done something stupid and opened a socket or a file somewhere in that 10k+ SLoC.Therefore we need a very clear demarcation between computation and side effects. In Othismo that takes the shape of the image definition files (.oth) which describe the namespace + various type definitions describing what the interface of an object (should) be. It's somewhat like TypeScript, we don't actually do anything to verify an object conforms to this interface.I'd love your feedback on the syntax used to define images overall, I feel like it doesn't do a great job giving me a clear notion of the environment lexically. 
I'm more comfortable about the syntax for describing the behavior of objects, although things like `operator` and `readonly` are really only necessary because I've not done anything to support auth at the protocol layer yet.You can run the same website hosted at othismo.com with`git clone git@github.com:mamidon/othismo.git``task run:example:static`You can also play with the namespace interactively with```
task build:example:static
target/debug/othismo shell examples/static/static.rti# print out the namespace(s)
target/debug/othismo --check examples/static/static.rti
```You'll need rust, task (it's like make), and node+npm.

extra.story_text:
Othismo is a runtime which has a bunch of sandboxed WASM modules talking to each other + the host environment. It's actually hosting its own website right now at othismo.com.This is a project that's been percolating in my head for a while, as a vague desire to make a "better" runtime for software development. But it was never particularly clear for me what that would _actually_ look like. In the last month or so, I felt a bit inspired to ask what such a runtime might look like for agentic development.My hypothesis is that we really can't review 10k+ SLoC pull requests consistently and really understand them. But if we try to have a higher level view of things, we still can't be confident the agent(s) haven't done something stupid and opened a socket or a file somewhere in that 10k+ SLoC.Therefore we need a very clear demarcation between computation and side effects. In Othismo that takes the shape of the image definition files (.oth) which describe the namespace + various type definitions describing what the interface of an object (should) be. It's somewhat like TypeScript, we don't actually do anything to verify an object conforms to this interface.I'd love your feedback on the syntax used to define images overall, I feel like it doesn't do a great job giving me a clear notion of the environment lexically.

body:
# arumadev/aruma

Self-hosted backend compatible with the official Firebase SDKs. One Go binary and PostgreSQL.

- Stars: 5
- Forks: 0
- Watchers: 5
- Open issues: 0
- License: Apache License 2.0
- Homepage: https://arumadev.github.io/aruma/
- Default branch: main
- Created: 2026-10-17T20:43:27Z

## Languages

- Astro
- CSS
- Dart
- Dockerfile
- Go
- HTML
- Java
- JavaScript
- Makefile
- Objective-C
- PLpgSQL
- Python
- Ruby
- Shell
- Svelte
- Swift
- TypeScript

## Topics

- authentication
- backend-as-a-service
- firebase
- firebase-alternative
- golang
- open-source
- postgresql
- realtime-database
- self-hosted

## Top Contributors

- osama300 (1074 contributions)

---

## README

 

 
 
 
 

 

**A self-hosted backend that speaks the official Firebase SDKs.**
One Go binary and PostgreSQL. Your apps keep the official SDKs; a few platforms need a small helper (see SDK packages).

 

License
Go
PostgreSQL
Status

Quick start · Status · Docs · SDK packages · Contributing

 

 

## What Aruma is

Aruma is a self-hosted replacement for Firebase. It is one Go binary with PostgreSQL and an embedded Next.js dashboard. It serves Firebase Auth, Realtime Database, Cloud Storage, Security Rules and the Document Database (Firestore-compatible) to the official Firebase SDKs, so for Auth, Realtime Database and Firestore on supported setups you change a config file and not your application code. Storage on iOS uses a patched build of the Storage SDK, Flutter Storage needs one helper call (`fromArumaUrl`), and servers that verify ID tokens use Aruma's admin libraries. See SDK packages.

It is for developers and teams who use Firebase and want to run the backend themselves, on a small VPS or on their own servers, with their data in a PostgreSQL they control.

Behavior is checked against real Firebase and the official emulators, and the official Firebase test suites run against Aruma. Differences we know of are documented in known differences.

## Status

Aruma is pre-1.0. The latest release is v0.4.0. Part of the Document Database's verification has not run yet; the changelog lists it.

| Service | Status | Details |
|---|---|---|
| Platform: projects, apps, API keys, service accounts, dashboard, Management API | Released | Architecture |
| Authentication | Released in v0.1.0 | Compatibility, web guide, Admin guide |
| Realtime Database | Released in v0.2.0, off by default (`ARUMA_RTDB_ENABLED`) | Compatibility, guide |
| Security Rules | Released in v0.3.0 | Compatibility, guide |
| Cloud Storage | Released in v0.3.0, off by default (`ARUMA_STORAGE_ENABLED`) | Compatibility, guide |
| Document Database (Firestore-compatible) | Released in v0.4.0, off by default (`ARUMA_DOCUMENTS_ENABLED`); official mobile suites not run yet | Compatibility, guide, migration guide |
| Cloud Messaging, App Check, Remote Config, Functions | Planned | |

## Quick start

With Docker (Aruma and PostgreSQL 18, nothing else to install):

```bash
git clone --branch v0.4.0 https://github.com/arumadev/aruma.git && cd aruma
printf 'ARUMA_MASTER_KEY=%s\nPOSTGRES_PASSWORD=%s\n' "$(openssl rand -base64 32)" "$(openssl rand -hex 24)" > .env
docker compose up -d
docker compose logs aruma | grep code    # the one-time setup code
```

Open, enter the setup code to create your first account, then create a project and an app and copy the config file. Keep `.env`: every key Aruma uses is derived from `ARUMA_MASTER_KEY`.

Without Docker, download the archive for your system from Releases (Linux, macOS and Windows, amd64 and arm64) and point it at your PostgreSQL 18, or build from source with Go 1.27.3 and Node 24 (`make dashboard && make dev`).

Getting started goes on from here: the three ways to install, running on a server, creating a project and an app, and signing a user in from a web app. Settings are in configuration.

## How apps connect

Your app keeps the official SDK and takes the config file from Aruma. Where a platform has Google's hosts compiled in, a small package under `sdk/` points the SDK at your server with one line of build or manifest configuration. The packages and what each one does are in SDK packages.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph Apps["Your apps, official Firebase SDKs"]
        W[Web]
        I[iOS]
        A[Android]
        F[Flutter]
        N[Admin: Node, Go]
    end
    Apps -- "same SDK, new config" --> E
    subgraph Aruma["Aruma, one Go binary"]
        E[Single entry point] --> Auth
        E --> RTDB[Realtime Database]
        E --> Storage[Cloud Storage]
        E --> Docs[Document Database]
        E --> Console[Dashboard and Management API]
    end
    Auth --> PG[(PostgreSQL)]
    RTDB --> PG
    Storage --> PG
    Docs --> PG
    Console --> PG
```

Every project's data is reached through its project number, directly or through a project-scoped parent such as a Realtime Database id. A CI test fails any SQL query on a project table that neither filters by project nor carries a reviewed scope annotation. Aruma does not use PostgreSQL row-level security. See architecture.

**Cloud Functions.** Aruma does not serve Cloud Functions. If an app signs in with Aruma Auth and calls a function with `httpsCallable`, the SDK sends the user's Aruma ID token to Google. Do not use callable functions in such an app. See known differences.

## The dashboard

Every Aruma server ships with a dashboard, embedded in the same binary. Create projects and apps, manage users, edit rules, browse data and files, and download the config files your apps need.

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 

## Documentation

- Getting started
- Documentation index
- Guides: web Auth, Admin Auth, Realtime Database, Cloud Storage, security rules, Firestore, Firestore migration, mobile apps, operations
- Reference: configuration, compatibility, known differences, console API
- Architecture, security, testing, benchmarks
- Changelog

To report a vulnerability, read SECURITY.md.

## Contributing

Issues and pull requests are welcome. Start with CONTRIBUTING.md.

## License

Apache License 2.0, see LICENSE and NOTICE. Firebase is a trademark of Google LLC. Aruma is not affiliated with Google and is not endorsed by it.

title: Show HN: NES Contra (1987) port (ASM –> C and then C –> WebAssembly)
author: tevlon
body: Based on vermiceli's annotated disassembly of Contra: https://github.com/vermiceli/nes-contra-us. Thanks for the great work.I ported it in two steps. First to C: the game logic is translated routine by routine from the 6502 assembly, and checked frame by frame against the original in the Mesen emulator. Then the C code to WebAssembly so it runs in the browser.The cherry on top: online multiplayer, so two players can play co-op over the internet.Source: https://github.com/epoyraz/nes-contra-us

comments.author: tevlon
comments.text: For the Multiplayer part: It's deterministic lockstep. Both browsers run the same C core (compiled to WebAssembly), and the only thing sent over the network is each player's button bitmask per frame. Local input is delayed by 4 frames (~67 ms), which hides normal internet latency; if the other player's input for a frame hasn't arrived yet, the game waits for it. Every 2 seconds both sides compare a hash of the game RAM to catch desyncs. Transport is a WebRTC data channel via PeerJS (its free cloud server handles matchmaking with a room code), with Google's STUN server for NAT traversal and Metered's free-tier TURN relay as a fallback when a direct connection isn't possible.For AI usage: It was all done by Claude/Codex, but it wasn't that straight forward. First: i started in April and the models weren't good enough and would make errors. You could see those immediately in glitches. Then, i spent some time in building a harness and collect telemetry data in Mesen. Once, i had that: i just played the game in the emulator and asked Claude Opus 5.5 to use this as verification. The rest was smooth.

Some games use RAM, which makes it harder as you'd have to index the PNG by hash or something.

First to C: the game logic is translated routine by routine from the 6502 assembly, and checked frame by frame against the original in the Mesen emulator. title: Show HN: [Pulse] Thanks to C, I have a project with which I am happy
author: xerrs
body: I have been dabbling with programming ever since Covid was a thing. And since then I jumped around and programmed a lot of stuff, whether it was Websites, Apps or simple Python programs. Unfortunately, I have never really gotten that "feel", the feel of being useful or something like that. Most of the projects I have done, died out, and the issue was not just that my programs were not reaching anybody, it was also that I felt like I was not learning anything.Then came C, and I just have to say, that it was probably one of the best decisions I have ever made. I have tried C a lot, once I was 15, 17, and now, 19 years old. This time it stuck with me, and moved me to create my own organization called cherries.works, with the sole focus of creating efficient, open source, free and simple tools for developers.After more than 5 contributions, issues created, bugs fixed, letting it run on my own homelab for 4-5 hours, I can confidently say, that with the help of C, my biggest project Pulse was made ( https://github.com/cherries-works/pulse ).I was vacating somewhere and left my laptop at home. I brainstormed a lot about creating this organization during my vacation, and my project Pulse. This is around 6 months ago. And now after 6 months, seeing how well everything turned, really makes me happy.Might be far-fetched, but as someone who has learned multiple languages, coded in multiple areas, and created (way) too many projects, I can confidently say, that thanks to C, I have a project that actually makes me happy.Pulse is a simple monitoring tool that does not require you to sign in, or setup anything. You just download it with a single curl command, and run it on your device. I created it because I really dont like the setup hell, or whatever it takes to get a single monitoring tool running, and also because I wanted to learn C, not to mention having a program I control would mean I can add my features I would want (such as quick web hosting, API sharing, JSON formatting, styling etc.). At the end, it really was a win-win for me.Would mean a lot if devs who are interested could check it out, and point me towards some issues that I could fix, as I feel like the project is reaching a stagnation point. But even then, I am just really happy to look at Pulse, and be able to say, that *I, me* are the one who programmed that.

Yes. Your name, email and the subscriptions you add. No banking data. You can export everything as CSV or delete your account from inside the app at any time.

Anytime, in Account → Manage subscription. Pro stays active until the end of the period you've paid for, then your account goes back to Free without losing any data.

## README

 
 
 
 
 

# @khalilgharbaoui/opencode-claude-code-plugin

**Claude Code is the provider.** This opencode plugin runs Anthropic's Claude models through the official **Claude Code CLI** (`claude`) as a subprocess instead of calling the HTTP API. opencode inherits whatever that CLI is logged in as (a Claude subscription, an API key, Bedrock or Vertex), gets Claude's own tools, MCP servers and skills, and keeps running the tools that touch your machine itself, behind its own permission prompts. One package serves opencode 1.x and 2.x.

- **Your CLI's login, untouched.** The plugin never reads, stores or replays a token. Lifting the OAuth session out of the official client is what proxy-style plugins do, and Anthropic disallowed that for third-party Claude use in February 2026. This plugin structurally cannot do it.
- **opencode runs the tools.** `Bash`, `Edit`, `Write`, `WebFetch` and `Task` are proxied by default: Claude calls an in-process MCP tool and opencode executes it, under its own permissions and audit log.
- **Billed as your CLI bills.** Headless `claude --print` on a subscription draws from the plan's ordinary usage limits; an API key bills pay as you go. The CLI's `apiKeySource` says which, every session, and the plugin warns when a stray `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` would move the bill.

**Docs:** (the same pages are the markdown under `docs/`, which GitHub renders on its own).

## Quickstart

1. **Install and log in the Claude Code CLI.** The plugin drives an existing `claude`; it does not bundle one.

   ```bash
   claude --version      # e.g. 2.1.284 (Claude Code)
   claude auth status    # which account you are signed in as
   claude auth login     # only if you are not signed in yet
   ```

2. **Add the package to opencode's global config.** That spec is the whole install. Do not `npm install` it yourself: opencode resolves and caches plugin packages on its own.

   ```json
   {
     "plugin": ["@khalilgharbaoui/opencode-claude-code-plugin"]
   }
   ```

 `~/.config/opencode/opencode.json` on opencode 1.x. opencode 2 reads the same key; its native spelling is `plugins`.

3. **Quit opencode fully and relaunch.** Plugins load once, at process start. The model picker now has a **Claude Code (Default)** provider with entries such as `Claude Sonnet 5.5 (2×)` and `Claude Opus 5 (5×)`; the suffix is each model's list price relative to Haiku.

Nothing in the picker? Troubleshooting is keyed on the first thing you see. `/claude-code-doctor` in any session prints what the plugin thinks is happening, without calling a model.

## What you get

| | |
|---|---|
| **Selective tool proxy** | Choose, per tool, whether Claude Code or opencode executes it. Proxied calls end on an event (the result, an abort, the next message, the child exiting), never on a clock. Guide |
| **Claude's own tools, MCP and skills** | `Read`, `Grep`, `Glob`, `WebSearch` run in Claude Code; your opencode MCP servers are bridged in; your opencode skills can be staged for Claude's `Skill` tool. MCP · Skills |
| **Several accounts** | `"accounts": ["personal", "work"]` becomes one provider per account. Out of usage mid-task? One line says which account, which window and when it resets in your own time zone, and names the others to pick a model from. Accounts |
| **Subagents: your account, their model** | `forceModel`, `reasoningEffort` and `cacheTtl` in an agent file, inheriting the caller's account. `task_batch` runs several subagents at once. Subagents |
| **The whole model range, reasoning variants, fast mode** | Haiku 4.5 through Opus 5.5, Fable and Mythos, each with a `(N×)` list-price suffix, `low` to `max` effort variants, and a fallback chain for a model this account cannot run today. The badge above counts them. Models |
| **`/btw` and `/claude-code-doctor`** | Side questions on the live process, and a health report whose `bundle` form is redacted by allowlist so it is safe to paste into a public issue. `/btw` · Doctor |
| **Ships its own setup skill** | Ask Claude to configure it. The bundled `claude-code-plugin` skill knows every option, env var, model id and troubleshooting rule, is staged into Claude Code on every spawn, and tests keep it in step with the code. Skills |
| **Read-only preset, plan mode** | `"permissionPreset": "read-only"` holds at the CLI, the proxy and the permission layer at once. Permissions |

## How this compares

| | opencode's native `anthropic` provider | This plugin | Proxy and token-reuse plugins |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Authentication** | A Platform API key in opencode's auth store. | Whatever the official `claude` CLI holds. No token is read, stored or replayed. | The Claude OAuth session, used outside the official client. |
| **Terms-of-service status** | The ordinary API route. | Sanctioned: the official client does the authenticating. | Disallowed. Anthropic disallowed reusing subscription authentication for third-party Claude use in February 2026, and each of those projects carries its own disclaimer. |
| **Who runs Bash, Edit, Write** | opencode. | opencode, by default; `Read`, `Grep`, `Glob` run in Claude Code. | opencode. |
| **What it costs you** | Baseline. | A `claude` child per conversation under a cap of 16; Claude Code may compact its own context behind opencode's back. | One more moving part, plus the account risk above. |

The full comparison has nine rows, names the projects in the third column, and quotes their own READMEs.

## Built from measurements

A dozen test files drive a fake `claude` through real turns: the stream parser, the proxy broker, both watchdogs, abort, respawn, account failover and the model fallback chain are exercised end to end. Every rule in `AGENTS.md` names the probe, the version and the number that produced it, and the evidence lives in `docs/agents-history.md`. Two runtime dependencies. The site reports the live numbers: it rebuilds itself after every release, on every push that moves a figure, and every six hours.

## Documentation

- **Start here:** Introduction · Getting started · opencode 2 · Models · Billing
- **Configuration:** Options · Environment variables · Accounts · Subagents · Permissions · MCP · Skills · Logging
- **Guides:** Tool proxy · Background subagents · `/btw` · `/claude-code-doctor` · Per-turn stats · Compaction and thinking · Interactive transport · Other plugins
- **Troubleshooting:** Start from the symptom · Longer cases · Which login bills what · Known limitations
- **Internals:** How a turn works · How a proxied call ends · Scratch files and security · Measurement culture · Testing · Development · Releasing

### Where the old README sections went

This README used to hold all of the above. Release notes and bookmarks point at its anchors, so:

| Old README anchor | Now at |
|---|---|
| `#configuration`, `#options-reference` | docs/configuration/options.md |
| `#environment-variables` | docs/configuration/environment.md |
| `#models`, `#fast-mode` | docs/models.md |
| `#multiple-claude-code-accounts`, `#account-failover` | docs/configuration/accounts.md |
| `#billing` | docs/billing.md |
| `#troubleshooting` | docs/troubleshooting/symptoms.md |
| `#plugin-health-with-claude-code-doctor` | docs/guides/doctor.md |
| `#selective-tool-proxy` | docs/guides/tool-proxy.md |
| `#credits` | docs/credits.md |

## Credits

Made and maintained by Khalil Gharbaoui (@khalilgharbaoui). This plugin absorbs work from its forks directly, cherry-picked with the original authorship preserved or reimplemented with the author named in the commit. The people behind the features you are using, and what each built, are on the Credits page; `git log --author` on this repo shows the preserved authorship.

## Support

This plugin is maintained, not a side project that gets abandoned when the next Claude Code or opencode release breaks something. Keeping it working means tracking CLI flag changes, opencode plugin API changes, and new model IDs as they ship.

If the plugin saves you time, you can keep it maintained here:

 

One-off or recurring, both help. Bug reports and PRs are welcome too; see `AGENTS.md` for the contribution rules.

## License

MIT. See LICENSE. The first version was written by Émilien (@unixfox); everything since by Khalil Gharbaoui and the people in Credits.

body:
ACID-211
 An acid machine by Hektor Qafarov (QAFARØV). Synthesizers, sequences and liquid.
 ACID-211 is an audiovisual artwork and a free browser-based music instrument. Its acid-green liquid surface contains a step sequencer, kick, bass, acid synthesizer and hats. Listen to the demo on the opening screen, then select START to make your own loop.
 On desktop, edit patterns across four sections, choose instrument presets, shape sounds with oscillators and envelopes, and combine Corrode and Mutate effects. Space toggles playback. On phones, the opening composition offers demo playback; the sequencer requires a desktop display.
 The live liquid graphics require WebGL2 and JavaScript. Sound is generated in your browser.

title: Show HN: Maclet – A native macOS container runtime written from scratch in Rust
author: paperplaneflyr
body:
# sumant1122/maclet

Native macOS container runtime written in Rust using Apple Virtualization Framework, Linux namespaces, cgroups v2, and OverlayFS

- Stars: 4
- Forks: 0
- Watchers: 4
- Open issues: 0
- License: Apache License 2.0
- Default branch: main
- Created: 2026-10-31T03:30:52Z

## Languages

- C
- Makefile
- Rust
- Swift

## Topics

- apple-silicon
- cgroups-v2
- container-runtime
- containers
- linux-namespaces
- macos
- oci
- overlayfs
- rust
- virtualization

## Top Contributors

- sumant1122 (10 contributions)

---

## README

# Maclet

**Maclet** is a native macOS container runtime written in Rust. It creates, runs, and isolates Linux containers without depending on Docker Desktop, Colima, or containerd.

> **The Elevator Pitch:** 
> *Docker Desktop on macOS is a multi-gigabyte, proprietary suite wrapping legacy orchestration daemons. **Maclet** is a native, ultra-lightweight container runtime written from scratch in Rust and Swift specifically for Apple Silicon. Instead of wrapping Docker Engine or containerd, Maclet talks directly to Apple's Virtualization Framework and implements Linux kernel isolation primitives (namespaces, cgroups v2, OverlayFS, and bridge networking) with zero bloat and sub-second boot times.*

---

## Key Differentiators: What Makes Maclet Unique?

| Dimension | Docker Desktop | Colima / Lima | **Maclet** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Core Engine** | Docker Daemon + `containerd` + `runc` | QEMU / Lima + `containerd` | **Ground-up Rust runtime (Direct Linux Syscalls)** |
| **VM Backend** | HyperKit / Apple VZ (Heavy VM) | QEMU / Apple VZ | **Apple Virtualization Framework via Swift C-FFI** |
| **Idle Memory** | ~2.0 GB – 4.0 GB | ~800 MB – 1.5 GB | **< 150 MB** |
| **Binary Size** | ~1.5 GB+ (with Electron) | Hundreds of MBs | **~3.6 MB (Single Rust binary)** |
| **Boot Time** | 10 – 30+ seconds | 5 – 15 seconds | **Sub-second (~800ms)** |
| **Dependency Model** | Wraps existing engines | Wrapper script around containerd | **Independent: Owns namespaces, cgroups, OverlayFS & OCI** |
| **Licensing** | Proprietary paid subscription | Open source | **100% Free & Open Source (Apache 2.0 / MIT)** |

---

## Architecture Overview

```
maclet CLI (macOS)
       │
       ▼ (Unix Domain Socket: ~/.maclet/maclet.sock)
maclet Daemon / maclet-vm
       │
       ▼ (Apple Virtualization Framework via Swift C-FFI)
Linux ARM64 Guest VM
       │
       ▼ (Virtio Console Channel: /dev/hvc1)
maclet-guest-agent (Rust static binary as PID 1)
       │
       ├─► Linux Namespaces (PID, Mount, Net, IPC, UTS)
       ├─► cgroups v2 Quotas (cpu.max, memory.max, pids.max)
       ├─► Storage: OverlayFS (lower/upper/work/merged) & pivot_root
       ├─► Network: maclet0 Bridge, Veth pairs, Netns, NAT Masquerading, Port Forwarding
       ├─► Security: Capability bounding set dropping, PR_SET_NO_NEW_PRIVS, Read-Only Rootfs
       └─► Containerized Processes
```

---

## Features Implemented Across All 8 Phases

| Phase | Subsystem | Features |
|---|---|---|
| **Phase 1** | **VM Boot & IPC** | Apple Virtualization Framework backend (`apple-vz` Swift FFI), ARM64 Linux VM boot, Virtio console IPC channel (`/dev/hvc1`), newline-delimited JSON RPC protocol. |
| **Phase 2** | **First Container** | Direct Linux process isolation (`CLONE_NEWPID`, `CLONE_NEWNS`, `CLONE_NEWUTS`, `CLONE_NEWIPC`), `pivot_root`, fresh `/proc`, `/sys`, `/dev` mounts. |
| **Phase 3** | **Resource Controls** | cgroups v2 hierarchy (`/sys/fs/cgroup/maclet/`), memory limits (`--memory`), CPU quotas (`--cpus`), process limits (`--pids-limit`), live metrics accounting (`maclet stats`). |
| **Phase 4** | **Container Lifecycle** | Detached background containers (`-d`), multiple concurrent containers, container ID prefix/name matching, `maclet ps -a`, `maclet exec` (via `setns()`), `maclet logs`, `maclet inspect`, `maclet stop`, `maclet rm -f`. |
| **Phase 5** | **Storage & Image Management** | OCI registry client with multi-arch manifest resolution (`linux/arm64`), streaming layer download & SHA256 verification (`maclet pull`), local image registry (`maclet images`), OverlayFS copy-on-write storage per container. |
| **Phase 6** | **Container Networking** | `maclet0` Linux bridge (`10.88.0.1/16`), IPAM allocation, veth pairs moved to container netns, loopback & default gateway routing, guest NAT masquerading, automatic DNS configuration, and port forwarding (`-p host:container`). |
| **Phase 7** | **Security & Hardening** | Capability bounding set dropping (`CAP_SYS_ADMIN`, `CAP_SYS_MODULE`, etc.), `PR_SET_NO_NEW_PRIVS` enforcement, immutable root filesystems (`--read-only`), hypervisor isolation boundary. |
| **Phase 8** | **Production Readiness** | System diagnostics (`maclet system info`), comprehensive unit tests, end-to-end VM boot and execution test suite (`make test`), complete architecture and subsystem documentation. |

---

## Project Structure

```text
maclet/
├── Cargo.toml
├── Makefile
├── README.md
├── LICENSE
├── entitlements.plist
│
├── docs/
│   ├── architecture.md           # System architecture & data flow
│   ├── technical-constraints.md  # Darwin limits & hypervisor workarounds
│   ├── apple-vz-research.md      # Apple Virtualization Framework internals
│   ├── kernel-configuration.md   # Minimum Linux kernel config
│   ├── host-guest-protocol.md    # Framed JSON wire protocol spec
│   ├── container-lifecycle.md    # Container state machine & OverlayFS
│   ├── crate-boundaries.md       # Rust crate dependency structure
│   ├── security.md               # Hardware/kernel security model & capabilities
│   ├── networking.md             # Bridge, veth, netns, NAT & port forwarding
│   ├── vm-management.md          # VM configuration, booting & lifecycle
│   ├── implementation-roadmap.md # Phased implementation roadmap
│   └── risk-analysis.md          # Architectural risks & mitigations
│
├── crates/
│   ├── maclet-common/            # Protocol models, errors, container configs
│   ├── maclet-ipc/               # Async & sync newline-framed JSON stream
│   ├── maclet-vm/                # Apple Virtualization Framework Rust wrapper
│   ├── maclet-cli/               # CLI interface (clap) & daemon manager
│   ├── maclet-namespaces/        # Linux namespace unshare & pivot_root
│   ├── maclet-cgroups/           # Linux cgroups v2 controllers & resource metrics
│   ├── maclet-storage/           # Linux OverlayFS storage & COW layers
│   ├── maclet-network/           # Bridge, veth pair, netns, NAT & port forwarding
│   ├── maclet-image/             # OCI image pull, layer unpack & registry
│   ├── maclet-container/         # Container state machine & supervisor
│   └── maclet-guest-agent/       # Statically linked Linux init & agent
│
├── virtualization/
│   └── apple-vz/                 # Swift FFI wrapper around VZVirtualMachine
│       ├── include/apple_vz.h
│       └── Sources/apple_vz.swift
│
└── guest/                        # Kernel and initramfs tooling
```

---

## Quickstart

### Prerequisites

1. macOS running on Apple Silicon (ARM64).
2. Xcode Command Line Tools (`xcode-select --install`).
3. Rust (`rustup default stable` and `rustup target add aarch64-unknown-linux-musl`).

### Build & Test

```bash
# Build release binaries (CLI and guest agent) and sign with virtualization entitlement
make release

# Run all unit tests and the end-to-end VM boot and execution test
make test
```

---

## CLI Command Reference

### VM Machine Management

```bash
# 1. Initialize environment (prepares Linux kernel, minirootfs & builds guest agent)
maclet machine init

# 2. Start the Linux micro-VM in the background
maclet machine start --daemon

# 3. Check VM and guest agent status
maclet machine status

# 4. Inspect system info and hypervisor status
maclet system info

# 5. Stop the VM
maclet machine stop
```

### Image Management

```bash
# Pull an OCI image from Docker Hub / registry
maclet pull alpine:latest
maclet pull ubuntu:24.04

# List locally cached images
maclet images
```

### Container Execution & Lifecycle

```bash
# Run an ephemeral container
maclet run alpine:latest uname -a

# Run a detached background container with custom name and port forwarding
maclet run -d --name web-server -p 8080:80 alpine:latest /bin/sh -c "while true; do sleep 1; done"

# Run with resource limits (cgroups v2)
maclet run --memory 256m --cpus 1.5 --pids-limit 50 alpine:latest /bin/sh

# Run with hardened security (read-only rootfs)
maclet run --read-only alpine:latest /bin/sh

# List running containers (or all containers with -a)
maclet ps
maclet ps -a

# Execute a command inside a running container (via namespaces setns)
maclet exec web-server ps aux

# View container logs
maclet logs web-server

# Inspect container state and configuration
maclet inspect web-server

# View live cgroup resource statistics (CPU, Memory, PIDs)
maclet stats web-server

# Stop a running container
maclet stop web-server

# Remove a container
maclet rm -f web-server
```

---

## Running Automated Tests

```bash
# Run the complete test suite (unit tests + e2e boot test)
make test
```

The test suite validates:
- IPC framed serialization and deserialization across sockets.
- OCI image reference parsing (Docker Hub, official library shortcuts, custom registries).
- Cgroups v2 controller path generation and metric parsers.
- Linux namespace unshare flags and configuration mapping.
- Swift FFI bridging and configuration validation.
- End-to-end VM boot, agent handshake, and command execution on Apple Silicon.

---

## Who is Maclet for?

1. **Apple Silicon Developers**: Engineers who want fast, responsive container workflows without their MacBook fans spinning up or battery draining from bloated virtualization stacks.
2. **Teams Looking to Escape Docker Licensing**: Organizations seeking to eliminate recurring per-seat Docker Desktop enterprise subscription fees while retaining high developer velocity.
3. **Systems & Rust Enthusiasts**: Developers who appreciate clean, auditable systems where the entire stack—from Swift hypervisor calls to Linux namespaces and cgroups—is written in clean, modern Rust with zero hidden daemon dependencies.

title: Show HN: Jointter – A daily word puzzle using dots and lines
author: proy87
body:
Hello everyone. I’m a mathematician by training, and I love mathematical and logical puzzles and brain-teasers. Inspired by popular games like Sudoku and Wordle, I decided to come up with an engaging game of my own.As it turns out, that’s not so easy! I had a few ideas, but beyond the core mechanics, a game also needs to be interesting and easy to explain — after all, nobody (including me) wants to spend a long time reading through rules.Let’s start with the concept, which came to me quite spontaneously: what if we represented letters like the digits on a digital clock — using lines, with dots at the points where those lines intersect? For instance, the letter "E" would consist of four lines and six dots — three at the intersections and three at the ends of the lines.It turns out that every letter of the Latin alphabet can be represented this way (with a minor caveat) using three rows of dots connected by some lines. This immediately presented a challenge: how do you represent O-shaped parts, like those found in "B", "O", or "R"? I decided not to use O-shapes, an use onl rectangles/squares. This "alphabet" is always displayed below the game board, so the player can see the letters.The goal of the game is simple: you are presented with three rows of dots and a set of lines, and you have to figure out the word. A great feature of the game is that it’s possible to deduce the word in a single turn — all the necessary information is right there on the board, allowing you to arrive at the answer with certainty.
And what if you can’t figure it out on the first try? You can enter a guess, much like in Wordle: if the lines from the entered word are part of the target word, they turn green; if not, they turn red. The same applies to the dots.
As you play, more and more lines gradually appear...Why provide some lines at the start? To uniquely identify a specific word — or a small set of words — from the dictionary. For example, you could select a configuration of lines that corresponds to only one word, like "RADIO", or perhaps to just two possible words, such as "WEIGH" and "WRONG".The rules seem clear, but the mechanics — not so much.
There are dots on the board; when I enter a word, I realize there aren't enough dots. What should I do? Initially, if the target word had 5 letters, I allowed users to enter 4- or 5-letter guesses, but that just confused players. So, I came up with a different solution: adding red dots for dots that aren't part of the target word.Another drawback is that the game is somewhat skewed. Since letters are processed from left to right, the first letters are revealed more frequently than the last ones.Then there’s the game design itself: should the target words be 5 letters long, or 6? Should a single board allow for multiple possible answers (like "WEIGH" and "WRONG"), or should it be limited to one — or perhaps more than two? Should the difficulty increase from Monday to Sunday? Currently, it’s set up this way: Monday is the easiest (a few 3-letter words), while Sunday is the hardest (more than two 7-letter words).The tech stack is simple: I use Flask for the backend and Python for the algorithms; I wrote the algorithms myself. While the JS, HTML, and CSS were created with the help of AI.I’d love for you to test the game and share what you like, what you don’t, and what could be improved.Specifically, I’d like to know:1. Is the game and its goal clear?2. Is it fun to play, and what could be improved?3. Would you share it with your friends?I welcome any constructive criticism.You can find the game at https://www.jointter.com/It’s free and requires no registration.Thank you very much.

extra.story_text:
Hello everyone. I’m a mathematician by training, and I love mathematical and logical puzzles and brain-teasers. Inspired by popular games like Sudoku and Wordle, I decided to come up with an engaging game of my own.As it turns out, that’s not so easy! I had a few ideas, but beyond the core mechanics, a game also needs to be interesting and easy to explain — after all, nobody (including me) wants to spend a long time reading through rules.Let’s start with the concept, which came to me quite spontaneously: what if we represented letters like the digits on a digital clock — using lines, with dots at the points where those lines intersect? For instance, the letter "E" would consist of four lines and six dots — three at the intersections and three at the ends of the lines.It turns out that every letter of the Latin alphabet can be represented this way (with a minor caveat) using three rows of dots connected by some lines. This immediately presented a challenge: how do you represent O-shaped parts, like those found in "B", "O", or "R"? I decided not to use O-shapes, an use onl rectangles/squares. This "alphabet" is always displayed below the game board, so the player can see the letters.The goal of the game is simple: you are presented with three rows of dots and a set of lines, and you have to figure out the word. A great feature of the game is that it’s possible to deduce the word in a single turn — all the necessary information is right there on the board, allowing you to arrive at the answer with certainty.
And what if you can’t figure it out on the first try? You can enter a guess, much like in Wordle: if the lines from the entered word are part of the target word, they turn green; if not, they turn red. The same applies to the dots.
As you play, more and more lines gradually appear...Why provide some lines at the start? To uniquely identify a specific word — or a small set of words — from the dictionary. For example, you could select a configuration of lines that corresponds to only one word, like "RADIO", or perhaps to just two possible words, such as "WEIGH" and "WRONG".The rules seem clear, but the mechanics — not so much.
There are dots on the board; when I enter a word, I realize there aren't enough dots. What should I do? Initially, if the target word had 5 letters, I allowed users to enter 4- or 5-letter guesses, but that just confused players. So, I came up with a different solution: adding red dots for dots that aren't part of the target word.Another drawback is that the game is somewhat skewed. Since letters are processed from left to right, the first letters are revealed more frequently than the last ones.Then there’s the game design itself: should the target words be 5 letters long, or 6? Should a single board allow for multiple possible answers (like "WEIGH" and "WRONG"), or should it be limited to one — or perhaps more than two? Should the difficulty increase from Monday to Sunday? Currently, it’s set up this way: Monday is the easiest (a few 3-letter words), while Sunday is the hardest (more than two 7-letter words).The tech stack is simple: I use Flask for the backend and Python for the algorithms; I wrote the algorithms myself. While the JS, HTML, and CSS were created with the help of AI.I’d love for you to test the game and share what you like, what you don’t, and what could be improved.Specifically, I’d like to know:1. Is the game and its goal clear?2. Is it fun to play, and what could be improved?3. Would you share it with your friends?I welcome any constructive criticism.You can find the game at https://www.jointter.com/It’s free and requires no registration.Thank you very much.

title: Show HN: A USB-C LTE modem that gives my computer a phone line
author: abijahkaj
body:
GitHub - Koppar-AI/koppar-lte-modem: A phone line over USB-C: LTE data, SMS and voice calls with the call audio on USB. A 4-layer KiCad board designed by Koppar from a one-page spec. · GitHub

A phone line over USB-C: LTE data, SMS and voice calls with the call audio on USB. A 4-layer KiCad board designed by Koppar from a one-page spec.

## Folders and files

| Name | Name | Last commit message | Last commit date |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| board | board | | |
| firmware | firmware | | |
| images | images | | |
| .gitignore | .gitignore | | |

# Koppar LTE modem: a phone line over USB-C

A 4-layer board that gives a computer its own phone line: LTE data, SMS and voice calls, with the call audio on USB. Plug in a nano-SIM and one USB-C cable, and the computer can answer a call through your headset, hand it to a script or an AI agent, or send a text.

The board was designed by Koppar from a one-page spec (`spec.txt`), then reviewed part by part against the datasheets.

## What it does

One USB-C cable, and the computer sees three ordinary devices through the on-board USB hub:

| Device | From | For |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Network adapter | Quectel EC25-EUX (U8) | LTE data, with 3G and 2G fallback (European bands) |
| Serial ports | EC25-EUX | AT commands: caller ID (`+CLIP`), texts (`AT+CMGS`), answer (`ATA`) |
| USB sound card | RP2040 (U5) | Call audio: the module's 1.8 V PCM interface, level-shifted, as a USB microphone and speaker |

There is no battery, screen or speaker. Three LEDs show NET (green), RING (amber) and CALL (blue). Power is 5 V from USB-C, a 3.8 V / 3 A buck for the module's 2 A transmit bursts, and 3.3 V for the hub, the RP2040 and its flash.

| Top | Back |
| --- | --- |
| | |

The schematic is also in PDF.

## What is here

| Path | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| `spec.txt` | The spec the board was designed from. |
| `board/` | KiCad 10 project: schematic, board, rules, the module footprint, symbol and 3D model. |
| `board/fab/` | Gerbers and drill files (`gerbers.zip`), IPC-2581, schematic PDF. |
| `board/fab/jlc/` | JLCPCB assembly BOM and placement files, with the part choices checked by hand. |
| `REVIEW.md` | The design review: what passed, what changed and why, ordering notes, what is still open. |
| `firmware/` | The RP2040 sound-card firmware (after bring-up). |

## Build one

Board. Upload `board/fab/gerbers.zip` to JLCPCB: 4 layers, 1.6 mm, stackup JLC04161H-3313 (the antenna feeds are 49 Ω on it). Every via is 0.45 / 0.2 mm and none sits in a pad, so pick Min via hole size 0.2mm/(0.3/0.35mm) and Via covering: Plugged: no via-in-pad, no extra options.

Assembly. Use `board/fab/jlc/BOM-JLCPCB.csv` and `CPL-JLCPCB.csv`. Glance at the placement preview before confirming, especially the LEDs and the SIM socket (the card slot is at the board edge). `REVIEW.md` lists the parts the files correct.

Parts you source yourself. These are not on JLCPCB's assembly line, or are not on the board at all:

| Part | What to get | Where |
| --- | --- | --- |
| U8, the LTE module | Quectel EC25-EUX, ordering code EC25EUXGR-128-SGNS (EC25EUXGA-128-SGNS is end-of-life; same LGA-144 footprint). It must be the EUX: the North American data-only variants have no voice. | Techship, DigiKey, Octopart (stock changes, check the suffix). Deselect U8 at assembly and solder it with hot air or a stencil, or consign it. |
| 2 antennas | LTE, 698 to 2690 MHz, U.FL (I-PEX MHF I), 50 Ω: one on MAIN (J3), one on DIV (J4) | e.g. Taoglas FXUB63 or Taoglas FXUB62.07.0150C |
| SIM | A nano-SIM with a voice plan | Your carrier |
| Cable and port | USB-C on both ends, from a port that offers 3 A at 5 V | The 5.1 kΩ CC resistors make the board a sink; they negotiate nothing, so a USB-A port or a 1.5 A source will brown out in a 2G burst |

## Open it in KiCad

Open `board/koppar-lte-modem.kicad_pro` in KiCad 10. The module's footprint, symbol and 3D model are in the project (`board/footprints`, `board/custom_syms`, `board/models`), wired in by the project's library tables.

KiCad's library has no 3D model for two of the footprints, so the 3D viewer shows them without a body:

| Part | Footprint | 3D model |
| --- | --- | --- |
| J1, USB-C receptacle | `Connector_USB:USB_C_Receptacle_HRO_TYPE-C-31-M-12` | LCSC C165948 (EasyEDA model) |
| J2, nano-SIM socket | `Connector_JAE:JAE_SIM_Card_SF72S006` | LCSC C2977286 (EasyEDA model) |

easyeda2kicad converts either one to a `.wrl` you can attach to the footprint. The renders above use them.

## Bring-up and recovery

There is no BOOTSEL button. A blank RP2040 boots into its USB bootloader anyway, and the back has three labelled pad groups for the rest:

- BOOT + GND: short them while plugging in and the RP2040 comes up as a USB drive for a new `.uf2`, even after a firmware that crashes before USB starts.
- SWD (CLK, DIO, GND): a Pico Debug Probe or any CMSIS-DAP probe.
- USB_BOOT + 1V8: short them while plugging in and the EC25 starts in emergency download mode, for a modem update that went wrong.

The modem does not switch itself on: the RP2040 drives its PWRKEY (GPIO22) and RESET_N (GPIO23). Until the firmware runs, the computer sees only the hub and the RP2040.

## The design review

The first version (rev A) had an antenna feed at 35 Ω that hopped layers, a buck 60 mm from its inductor, and a SIM socket facing the wrong way. All three are fixed here, along with the parts list and the assembly rotations. `REVIEW.md` has every finding with its numbers.

## Status

| Board | Rev B: 0 DRC errors, 0 unconnected, KiCad 10. Being ordered. |
| --- | --- |
| Next | Once the boards are built: bring-up, AT commands, the sound-card firmware, the first call and text. |

VoLTE is optional on the EC25-EUX. Where 2G and 3G are switched off, calls need a module firmware with VoLTE and a carrier that allows it; ask the seller.

## Design your own

This board started as a page of text. Koppar takes a spec like `spec.txt` to a schematic, a routed board, a BOM at live prices and Gerbers. It also takes a KiCad board you already have, or works from your own agent over MCP.

## Licence

CERN Open Hardware Licence Version 2, Permissive (`LICENSE`).

## About

A phone line over USB-C: LTE data, SMS and voice calls with the call audio on USB. A 4-layer KiCad board designed by Koppar from a one-page spec.

Cloud numbers get treated as VoIP, and old Android phones give you no clean way to get call audio in and out over USB.So this is a 4-layer USB-C board around a Quectel EC25-EUX. Behind a USB hub, the computer sees an LTE network adapter, the modem's AT serial ports (caller ID, SMS, answer), and an RP2040 acting as a USB sound card. The RP2040 bridges the modem's 1.8 V PCM audio through a level shifter. There's a 3.8 V buck sized for the 2 A GSM bursts, and no battery.I wrote the spec as one page of text, and Koppar, the tool I'm building, generated the schematic and the board. Then I reviewed it against the datasheets. The review found a 35 Ω antenna feed that hopped layers, a buck 60 mm from its inductor, and a SIM socket facing into the board. The parts matching would have bought an 18 µH inductor for a 4.7 µH slot. REVIEW.md in the repo has all of it with the numbers.Status: the boards aren't built yet. The repo is the design as I'm ordering it: KiCad 10 project, Gerbers, JLCPCB BOM and placement files. Bring-up and the sound-card firmware come next.Happy to answer anything about the audio path or the power design, and I'd like to hear what you'd change before the first bring-up.

comments.text: > Will LTE continue to work when 6G rolls out in 3 years?A significant change that came with LTE is the use of OFDM as the base of the air interface, which means that cellular providers no longer need to allocate large segments of spectrum to one protocol or another. Towers that were upgraded from 4G to 5G didn't need to disable 4G or consistently split their spectrum between the two they way they did when upgrading from 2G to 3G or 3G to 4G, they can dynamically allocate subchannels in each mode based on the immediate needs of their users.It seems unlikely that whatever technologies come in the future will regress in this way, so there shouldn't be a need for a hard cutoff at any point and I'd expect LTE devices to keep working for many generations to come.

title: Show HN: Similarity, a spiritual successor to 2000s-era OkCupid
author: stickfigure
body: This is a side project I've been working on on-and-off (mostly off) since the 1990s. I guess you would call it an experimental "dating site" though it's designed to be fun/interesting to people who aren't single (like me).You don't need to sign in to see how it works, so try it out. There is no swiping.The original inspiration was a 90s-era website called moviecritic.com that let you rate movies and get movie suggestions via collaborative filtering. I thought "hey, what about just matching me to the _people_ with the same taste instead?" And why just movies?The closest thing to this was 2000s-era OkCupid, before it was Tinderized. I want to capture its appeal, while making something novel.Similarity is not vibe coded, though I lean pretty heavily on codex (mostly the $20/mo plan - not a lot of tokens burnt here). The stack is java, guice/gwizard, elastic beanstalk, postgres (neon), react, jotai, and few cloudflare doodads. The match engine is a custom in-memory structure; getting the LLM to load test and optimize it was really a wow moment. Everything is PaaS and designed to scale by itself, cheaply, hands-off.I'm working on some ideas to help with the chicken/egg problem but for now I have low expectations. It's cheap to run and I have a day job.Would love feedback!

Was there something I was embarrassed about? Should I be? If so, should I fix that thing?I didn't really care about the dating aspect as much as the exercise in critical self evaluation.

The idea is that these would be conversation starters - if you both are passionate about skiing, it should be front and center.

title: Show HN: A language model that lives in a boot sector
author: kerlenton
body: All the ideas came from the boot sector demo scene where people had been writing chess and BASIC games in 512 bytes, even a C compiler. I wondered what one can do using a neural network instead of a program and generating boot logs for non-existent hardware was something fun to try.Entire inference engine is 510 bytes of MBR, weights, vocab, and strings reside in the sectors following MBR. Small char-level neural network was trained on dmesg generated by machine, so machine produces Linux boot messages infinitely.train.py performs precisely the same integer arithmetic operations as the asm code does and thus produces an output identical character-by-character to the one produced by QEMU. The difference analysis revealed my favorite bug. The characters at the beginning matched those generated by the simulator, but then the output diverged. I retrieved the hidden layer via QEMU’s debug port and compared the neurons' values with those of the simulator, one neuron at a time. Only the value of the first neuron was correct. The activation involves idiv, and idiv stores its remainder in edx. The pointer to the biases table was stored in edx, which resulted in the first neuron being biased correctly and the following ones using garbage. Now the bias' address is determined from the loop counter, and no pointers have to survive the division. Another bug I found simply by looking at the code before I did my first run-through: the BIOS print routine zeros out bx, but bx contains the predicted character number. This explains the push and pop of bx surrounding the print.sectorllm is the most similar to my project, as it runs an actual 5-layer llama2 with attention mechanism in just 1.2K of assembly code. It is the trade-off in the opposite direction, as my engine needs to fit into one sector and therefore my network has just one hidden layer of int8 operations for dreaming the dmesg.

comments.text: This is the kind of silly engineering that makes me appreciate humans.I need reminders sometimes that the world is filled with humans doing wierd things to share with one another.Not everything is about economic value or practicality. Making silly shit can be the goal.

# nicorobinreal/molehill

Mullvad as a rotating HTTP CONNECT proxy with sticky sessions and country support.

## Languages

- Go

## Top Contributors

- nicorobinreal (4 contributions)

---

## README

# molehill

Mullvad as a rotating connect proxy with sticky sessions and country support.

## Usage

1. Register a WireGuard key on your Mullvad account (needs `wg`, `curl`, `jq`):

   ```sh
   ACCOUNT=<your account number> && KEY=$(wg genkey) && \
   TOKEN=$(curl -s -X POST https://api.mullvad.net/auth/v1/token -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
     -d "{\"account_number\":\"$ACCOUNT\"}" | jq -r .access_token) && \
   IPV4=$(curl -s -X POST https://api.mullvad.net/accounts/v1/devices -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
     -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d "{\"pubkey\":\"$(echo "$KEY" | wg pubkey)\",\"hijack_dns\":false}" \
     | jq -r .ipv4_address)
   ```

2. Build and run the image:

   ```sh
   docker build -t molehill https://github.com/nicorobinreal/molehill.git#v0.1.0 && \
   docker run -d --name molehill --cap-add NET_ADMIN --sysctl net.ipv4.conf.all.src_valid_mark=1 \
     -p 127.0.0.1:8080:8080 -p 127.0.0.1:8081:8081 \
     -e MULLVAD_DEVICES="[{\"id\":\"d1\",\"private_key\":\"$KEY\",\"ipv4\":\"$IPV4\"}]" molehill
   ```

3. Send a request through a session named `s1` exiting in the US:

   ```sh
   curl -x 'http://session-s1-cc-us:x@localhost:8080' https://am.i.mullvad.net/json
   ```

The full reference (username format, configuration, response codes,
behavior, management API) is in docs.md.

title: Show HN: Tadpole – an LLM agent built from scratch then post-trained on 4B model
author: shakewingo
body:
# shakewingo/Tadpole

Build an LLM agent from scratch and continuously evolve it.

- Stars: 9
- Forks: 0
- Watchers: 9
- Open issues: 8
- License: MIT License
- Default branch: main
- Created: 2026-10-26T15:41:16Z

## Languages

- Jinja
- Jupyter Notebook
- Python
- Shell

## Topics

- agent
- from-scratch
- llama-cpp
- rl
- sft
- telegrambot
- tutorials

## Top Contributors

- shakewingo (79 contributions)

---

## README

# Tadpole

tests
Open In Colab
License: MIT
Hugging Face

*An LLM agent built from scratch, and grown one stage at a time.*

 
 
 

A tool-using agent in about 3,500 lines of plain Python, with no agent framework, that you can
run around the clock from Telegram, and a stage-by-stage record of how it was built, measured
and post-trained.

- **An agent you can use.** Files, shell, web search and fetch, sessions and compaction, on a
 local 4B model or any OpenAI-compatible API, in a terminal or as a Telegram bot.
- **A from-scratch tutorial.** Each stage adds one mechanism with tests and measured evidence,
 from the first agent loop to SFT, expert iteration and a GRPO pilot. Post-training lifts
 Qwen3-4B from **0.419 to 0.774** pass@1 on task types it never trained on
 (results).

## Use the agent

### Install

Python 3.11 or later. Run every command from the repository root with the venv active.

```sh
git clone https://github.com/shakewingo/Tadpole.git
cd Tadpole
python3 -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -e .
```

### Choose a model

Use a strong model through any OpenAI-compatible API: DeepSeek, OpenAI, OpenRouter, or your own
vLLM or LM Studio server. `export` these for the terminal, or put them in the
bot's env file:

```sh
export AGENT_BASE_URL=https://api.deepseek.com   # the API root; often ends in /v1
export AGENT_MODEL=deepseek-flash                # the provider's model ID
export AGENT_API_KEY=sk-...
export AGENT_N_CTX=32768                         # optional: the model's context window
```

 
 Run Qwen3-4B locally, base or post-trained: the model this project trains, for
studying the training rather than everyday use 

| Option | Variables |
|---|---|
| Ollama, any OS | `AGENT_BASE_URL=http://localhost:11434/v1`, `AGENT_MODEL=hf.co/unsloth/Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507-GGUF:Q4_K_M`, `AGENT_N_CTX=32768` |
| llama.cpp in-process, macOS; Qwen2 or Qwen3 GGUFs | leave `AGENT_BASE_URL` unset; `AGENT_MODEL_PATH` defaults to `models/Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507-Q4_K_M.gguf` |
| A Tadpole adapter on llama.cpp, macOS | `AGENT_MODEL_PATH=models/Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507-Q8_0.gguf`, `AGENT_LORA_PATH=models/ei-3-lora-f16.gguf` (or sft-1, sft-2); planning turns off, as in training |

```sh
# Ollama: pull, then serve with a window large enough for the agent
ollama pull hf.co/unsloth/Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507-GGUF:Q4_K_M
OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH=32768 ollama serve

# llama.cpp: the default AGENT_MODEL_PATH
hf download unsloth/Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507-GGUF Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507-Q4_K_M.gguf --local-dir models

# An adapter, on the Q8_0 base it was measured on
hf download unsloth/Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507-GGUF Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507-Q8_0.gguf --local-dir models
hf download Shakewin/tadpole-qwen3-4b-ei-3 ei-3-lora-f16.gguf --local-dir models
```

llama.cpp keeps the model in memory while the agent runs: about 8.5 GB for the Q8_0 base with its
32k window, which slows a 16 GB Mac.

 

### Chat in the terminal

```sh
python -m agent_from_scratch.agent
```

### Chat from Telegram

1. Message @BotFather with `/newbot` for a **bot token**, and
 @userinfobot for your numeric **user ID**.
2. Put both, and your `AGENT_*` variables if you use an API, in the env file:

   ```sh
   cp agent_from_scratch/deploy/telegram-bot.env.example agent_from_scratch/deploy/telegram-bot.env
   ```

3. Start it, and message your bot: `sh agent_from_scratch/scripts/run_telegram_bot.sh`

> [!WARNING]
> The agent runs shell commands and edits files with your user's permissions. It answers only
> `TELEGRAM_ALLOWED_USER_ID`, but anyone with the token controls the bot: keep the env file private.

In Telegram and the terminal: `/new` starts a session, `/reset` clears it, `/session `
switches to a named one, and `/compact` summarizes the history.

### Keep it running 24/7

Use an always-on machine: a Mac that does not sleep, a home server, or a small cloud VM with an
API model (1 GB is enough).

```sh
# Linux (systemd)
UNIT=~/.config/systemd/user/tadpole-bot.service
mkdir -p "$(dirname "$UNIT")" && cp agent_from_scratch/deploy/tadpole-bot.service "$UNIT"
sed -i "s|/REPLACE/WITH/REPO/PATH|$PWD|g" "$UNIT"
systemctl --user enable --now tadpole-bot && sudo loginctl enable-linger "$USER"

# macOS (launchd); also turn on "Prevent automatic sleeping when the display is off"
PLIST=~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.tadpole.telegram-bot.plist
cp agent_from_scratch/deploy/com.tadpole.telegram-bot.plist "$PLIST"
sed -i '' "s|/REPLACE/WITH/REPO/PATH|$PWD|g" "$PLIST"
mkdir -p outputs && launchctl load "$PLIST"
```

Logs: `journalctl --user -u tadpole-bot -f` on Linux, `outputs/telegram_bot.log` on macOS.

## Learn how it was built

Each stage adds one mechanism, with a deliberate failure, focused tests (601, none needing a
model) and evidence from real model runs.

| Stage | What you build | Code | Read and run |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0.5 | One request: model → tool call → result → answer, with validated calls and errors fed back | `llm.py`, `agent.py`, `tools/base.py` | notebook §1 |
| 1 | Multi-turn sessions, structured traces, explicit stop reasons | `session.py`, `trace.py` | notebook §2 |
| 2 | Files, shell, web search and fetch tools behind one registry | `tools/` | notebook §2 |
| 3 | Context budgeting, compaction, a summary checkpoint that survives restart | `context.py`, `compact.py` | notebook §3 |
| 8 | A generated benchmark, an independent verifier, a frozen protocol | `evals/bench/` | notebook §4, datasets, add a task type |
| 9 | SFT: verified trajectories → examples → LoRA adapter | `evals/sft/` | notebook §5–6, SFT data, training |
| 10 | Expert iteration and a GRPO pilot | `evals/sft/grpo.py` | notebook §7, EI and GRPO |
| 11 | One final comparison on held-out tests | `evals/report.py` | results |

Start with **the walkthrough notebook** (outputs
saved, so it reads on GitHub), then **the build log** for
each stage's evidence and **evaluating and post-training**
to run it yourself. Training needs a 24 GB CUDA GPU; the whole post-training line cost about
\$140 on RunPod.

## Post-training results

The agent's code, prompts and tools were frozen, with planning off (no `update_plan` tool); only
the weights changed. Every choice was made
on val, and each final model ran once on two held-out sets whose task types no training set
contains: 140 single-turn tasks (test) and 80 leveled tasks (hard test), three samples each.

| | Base | SFT-1 | SFT-2 | EI-3 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Test pass@1 | 0.419 | **0.774** | 0.738 | *0.745* |
| Test pass^3 (all three samples pass) | 0.364 | **0.707** | 0.607 | *0.657* |
| Hard test pass@1 | 0.275 | 0.429 | **0.492** | *0.471* |
| Hard test pass^3 | 0.125 | 0.250 | *0.325* | **0.338** |
| BFCL multi-turn† | *0.360* | 0.285 | 0.325 | **0.395** |

**Bold** is best, *italic* second. SFT-1: verified teacher trajectories plus When2Call and Toucan
rows. SFT-2: plus multi-turn demonstrations. EI-3: SFT-2 after three rounds of expert iteration.
† A local adaptation of BFCL's multi-turn base category, not a leaderboard score.

- **SFT on verified demonstrations gives the large gain**, and false "done" claims fall from 31
 to 1 in 420 runs.
- **The three post-trained models are level on held-out tasks** (0.648, 0.648, 0.645 over all
 220); EI-3 is the most balanced, and beats SFT-2 on BFCL (p = 0.034).
- **Val overstated expert iteration** (0.752 → 0.852), and **GRPO lost to it** at equal rollouts.
 Neither learned a behaviour the model never produced.

One training run per model, on a small local benchmark: not a claim about general agent ability.
Full tables, paired tests and limitations: docs/results.md.

### Download the adapters and data

Download all adapters and training data from Hugging Face.
Each card includes serving or data-reproduction instructions.

## Roadmap

- **Memory** across sessions, with remember, search and forget tools.
- **Skills and MCP** behind the same tool registry.
- **Background jobs** for the always-on bot, and a read-only sub-agent.
- **A self-improving harness**: with the model fixed, let execution feedback improve the prompts
 and tools.

Details: the build log.

The tool implementations adapt parts of nanobot
(attribution). Thanks to the authors of
Qwen3,
When2Call,
Toucan and
BFCL.

Apache-2.0, the SFT data MIT; see Third-party notices.

title: Show HN: A Kotlin compiler written in Go, 10x faster than kotlinc
author: barteo
body:
# barteo/kotlin-compiler-go

A Kotlin compiler for the JVM in Go, 10x faster than kotlinc

- Stars: 0
- Forks: 0
- Watchers: 0
- Open issues: 0
- License: Apache License 2.0
- Default branch: main
- Created: 2026-10-31T11:02:08Z

## Languages

- Go
- Java
- Python
- Shell

## Topics

- compiler
- go
- jvm
- kotlin

## Top Contributors

- barteo (1 contributions)

---

## README

# kotlin-compiler-go: a Kotlin compiler in Go

`kc` is a Kotlin compiler for the JVM, written in Go. On real libraries
it compiles 10x faster or more than `kotlinc` running in a warm JVM, and uses
about a tenth of the memory. The libraries it builds pass their own test
suites (Survey of real code), and it passes 95% of
`kotlinc`'s box tests (Conformance).

It is a prototype: it compiles most of Kotlin but not all of it, and it
checks less than `kotlinc` does (What it doesn't do).

## Results

`kc` against `kotlinc` 2.4.21 on an Apple M2 MacBook Air (8 cores, 16 GB),
JDK 21. `kotlinc` runs in a warm JVM, as it does in the Gradle daemon:
the median of repeated compilations in one JVM, after the JIT has warmed
up. `kc` uses all cores, as it does by default.

| Project | Files | Lines | `kotlinc` | `kc` | Speedup |
|:---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| kotlinpoet 2.4.0 | 39 | 8.7k | 1.23 s | 97 ms | **13x** |
| Ktor 3.6.0 (`ktor-io`, `ktor-utils`, `ktor-http`) | 236 | 24k | 2.32 s | 226 ms | **10x** |
| kotlinx-coroutines-core 1.11.0 | 169 | 34k | 2.50 s | 159 ms | **16x** |

- **On one core** (`kc -j 1`) `kc` is still 6.6–8.8x faster than warm
 `kotlinc`: 143 ms, 350 ms and 285 ms.
- **Cold**, with a new JVM per build as on the command line or in CI,
 `kotlinc` takes 6.9 s, 19.2 s and 10.9 s, 69–85x slower than `kc`.
- **Memory:** `kc` peaks at 85–118 MB, and cold `kotlinc`, with an 8 GB
 heap limit, at 1.0–1.1 GB.

How each number is measured, and the full tables with CPU time, are in
Benchmark.

## What it doesn't do

`kc` doesn't do all the work `kotlinc` does. It leaves out:

- **Some of the language.** A few features aren't supported, and
 visibility isn't checked. Unsupported Kotlin
 lists them all.
- **Most of `kotlinc`'s checks.** `kotlinc` runs 290 checkers for
 warnings and errors after type checking. `kc` has no separate
 checkers: it reports the errors that type checking finds, which is why
 it agrees with `kotlinc` on only 79% of the diagnostics tests.
- **Anything but the JVM.** There is no Kotlin/Native, JS or Wasm, and no
 language versions.
- **Incremental compilation, a Gradle plugin and IDE support.**
- **Identical output.** The class files work the same, but differ in
 places. For example, `kc` shares the objects of inline functions where
 `kotlinc` copies them, so it writes 790 classes for
 kotlinx-coroutines-core and `kotlinc` writes 850.
 Differences from kotlinc
 lists them.

The checkers don't explain the speedup. In a profile of both compilers
on one thread, `kc` is faster at each phase that both of them run:

| Work | `kotlinc` | `kc -j 1` | Ratio |
|:---|---:|---:|---:|
| Parsing | 4.7 s | 0.27 s | ~18x |
| Resolution and type checking | 8.8 s | 0.92 s | ~10x |
| Checkers (warnings and errors) | 5.4 s | none | |
| Reading the class path | 0.4 s | 0.01 s | |
| Backend, with inlining and writing | 19.1 s | 1.32 s | ~14x |
| **Total** | **38.4 s** | **2.51 s** | **15x** |

Even without its checkers, `kotlinc` would take 33 s, 13x as long as
`kc`. This profile is of 500 generated files (202k lines) in a warm JVM
(Where kotlinc's time goes).

## Why it's faster

- **No JVM.** `kc` starts in milliseconds; a cold `kotlinc` spends
 seconds starting the JVM and warming up the JIT.
- **Parallelism.** `kc` parses, checks bodies and generates class files
 on all cores; `kotlinc`'s frontend uses one.
- **Fewer passes.** `kotlinc`'s time is spread over 88 IR lowerings and
 290 checkers, none above about 2%. `kc` generates code in one pass
 over the checked AST.
- **Lazy inputs.** `kc` indexes the class path in about 5 ms while
 parsing, and decodes a class only when it's first used.

Design describes the pipeline.

## Try it

Requires Go 1.27.2+ and a JDK. The tests and benchmarks also need
`kotlinc` and `hyperfine` (`brew install go openjdk@21 kotlin hyperfine`).

```sh
go build -o bin/kc ./cmd/kc
bin/kc -d out testdata/run/fizzBuzz.kt
java -cp out FizzBuzzKt
```

`kc` doesn't add the standard library by itself. Put `kotlin-stdlib.jar`,
and any other libraries the program uses, on the class path to compile
and run it. For example, with kotlinx.coroutines, which ships with
`kotlinc`:

```sh
L=$(brew --prefix kotlin)/libexec/lib
CP=$L/kotlin-stdlib.jar:$L/kotlinx-coroutines-core-jvm.jar
bin/kc -cp $CP -d out testdata/run/stdlibCoroutinesBasics.kt
java -cp out:$CP StdlibCoroutinesBasicsKt
```

Arguments can be files or directories. Flags:

| Flag | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `-d` | output directory (default `.`) |
| `-cp`, `-classpath` | jars and directories to compile against |
| `-jdk-home` | JDK whose classes to use (default: `$JAVA_HOME`, or the JDK of `java` on `PATH`) |
| `-no-jdk` | don't use JDK classes |
| `-module-name` | module name, as in `kotlinc` (default `main`) |
| `-friend-paths` | class path entries whose internal declarations are visible (`kotlinc`'s `-Xfriend-paths`) |
| `-parcelize`, `-serialization`, `-compose` | apply the parcelize, kotlinx.serialization and Compose plugins |
| `-jvm-default` | how interface bodies compile, as in `kotlinc` (default `no-compatibility`) |
| `-Xdebug` | keep dead variables in suspend functions for debuggers, as in `kotlinc` |
| `-j` | parallel workers (default: all CPUs) |
| `-time` | print per-phase timings |
| `-features` | print each error with its unsupported feature, tab-separated |

There is no Gradle plugin. To try `kc` in a Gradle build, a Gradle init
script can replace a module's Kotlin compile task with a call to `kc`.
bench/kotlinpoet/kc.init.gradle.kts
does this for kotlinpoet.

### Repeat the benchmark

```sh
git clone --depth 1 --branch 1.11.0 https://github.com/Kotlin/kotlinx.coroutines.git \
  "${TMPDIR:-/tmp}/kc-survey/kotlinx-coroutines-1.11.0"
RUNS=5 WARM_RUNS=20 bench/coroutines-time.sh
```

`bench/coroutines-time.sh` builds `kc`, downloads the library's
dependencies from Maven Central, compiles it with both compilers using
its Gradle build's options, and writes the table to
bench/results/time-coroutines.md.
It expects `kotlinc` and the JDK where Homebrew installs them; set
`KOTLIN_HOME` and `JAVA_HOME` otherwise. `bench/kotlinpoet-time.sh` and
`bench/ktor-time.sh` time the other two libraries
(Benchmark).
## Documentation

- Unsupported Kotlin: what `kc` doesn't support, and
 where its output differs from `kotlinc`'s
- Design: the pipeline, type checking, class file
 generation, the inliner, coroutines and compiler plugins
- Benchmark: how `kc` is measured against `kotlinc`,
 and the results
- Survey of real code: which features real libraries use,
 and libraries built with `kc` and tested end to end
- Conformance: `kotlinc`'s own box and diagnostics
 tests run against `kc`

## Tests

```sh
go test ./...
```

Tests use the JDK in `$JAVA_HOME`, or the JDK of `java` on `PATH`. On macOS
`/usr/bin/java` is only a launcher, so set `JAVA_HOME`, for example
`export JAVA_HOME=$(/usr/libexec/java_home -v 21)`. Without a JDK, tests fail
with unresolved references to Java classes such as `HashMap`.

Tests that need the standard library find `kotlin-stdlib.jar` in
`$KOTLIN_HOME/lib` or next to `kotlinc` on `PATH`, and are skipped without
it. Tests that compare with `kotlinc` are skipped if it isn't on `PATH`. The
kotlinx.serialization 1.9.0 and Compose runtime 1.9.2 tests use jars from
Gradle's cache, or from `KC_SERIALIZATION_CP` and `KC_COMPOSE_CP`, and are
skipped without them.

- `testdata/run/`: programs compiled with `kc` and run under
 `java -Xverify:all`. Output must match `*.out`, which
 `testdata/gen_expected.sh` generates with `kotlinc`. A directory is a
 multi-file program with `main` in `main.kt`.
- `testdata/lib/`: a library compiled by `kc` and a program compiled
 against it by `kc` and by `kotlinc`. Both must produce `X.out`.
- `testdata/errors/`: each `// ERROR ` comment marks a line that must
 produce a diagnostic containing that text.
- `TestCoroutineShapes`: compares `kc`'s and `kotlinc`'s coroutine classes;
 differences must be listed in `testdata/coroutine-shapes.golden`.
- Package tests in `internal/` cover the parser, Kotlin metadata, class
 file frames and methods, the inliner and class path loading.

## License

Apache License 2.0, the same as `kotlinc`. See LICENSE.
