title: Show HN: Million Piece Puzzle
author: jeffbaumes
body: Show HN: Million Piece Puzzle

comments.author: jeffbaumes
comments.text: I love putting together puzzles, but I hardly ever get a chance to do puzzles with others. I made this simple game to experiment with a new type of puzzle experience at a grand scale. Everyone works together on a single puzzle. You log in with a color hex as your username. Each piece is a pixel of a 1000x1000 picture, which reveals as it gets built. Pieces are scattered randomly at first, and lock in when placed in the correct spot, at which point you automatically pick up the piece that was there and continue. Arrows guide you to the general area (hold a direction to move faster), but you still need to search the 5x5 target area for the correct exact location. The puzzle was constructed so each pixel is a different hex color, so it uses 1 million of the ~16 million possible colors in the picture. To make the image, I took a seed image and greedily assigned the closest available color to each pixel.

## README

 CVE Intel 

 
 Know which vulnerabilities matter, and what to do about them. 
 A private desktop app for vulnerability triage and scanning, written in native Rust, with a CLI, REST API and MCP server for developers and AI agents. 
 38 tools, 39 data sources, on-device AI.

 A 45-second, sped-up screen recording of the Windows app: CVE Triage, Compare CVEs, Scan dependencies, Threat landscape, Watchlist and the MCP server. Open the 1080p video. The screenshots below show the macOS app with live data from October 2026, in the light theme except for two in the dark theme. The app works the same on Windows and Linux. Click one to see it full size. 

## What is CVE Intel?

Every known software vulnerability gets a public ID, such as CVE-2024-3400,
and there are more of them than ever:
48,185 were published in 2025,
a fifth more than in 2024, and
2026 passed 84,000 before the end of October.
For each one, security, IT and development teams face the same question:
*does this affect us, and do we fix it now or can it wait?* Answering it
usually means checking NVD, CISA, FIRST, GitHub and vendor advisories by
hand, one browser tab at a time.

### Why it matters now

The places teams usually check are struggling to keep up. In April 2026,
NIST said
that the National Vulnerability Database can no longer analyse every CVE.
It now works first on CVEs in CISA's catalog of exploited vulnerabilities
(KEV) and in critical software, and no longer schedules its older backlog
for analysis. Attackers, meanwhile, are often faster than the fix:
Google's M-Trends 2026
found that the vulnerabilities attackers used were exploited, on average,
about a week *before* a patch was available, and that exploits have been
the most common way into networks for six years running.

So one database is no longer enough to decide what to patch. Checking
several independent sources, and fixing first what attackers are already
using, has become a vital part of keeping your systems safe. CVE Intel is
built to make that quick, private and free.

### What it does

CVE Intel does the legwork for you. Give it a vulnerability ID, a project
folder, a container image, the software on this computer, your own domains,
or a suspicious IP address, file hash or domain. It checks up to 39 public
security sources at once, including CISA KEV, FIRST's EPSS and ENISA's EU
Vulnerability Database alongside NVD. It comes back with one clear,
evidence-backed answer: what it is, how risky it is, whether attackers are
already using it, and what to do next. It also shows what changed this week
across those sources, and watches the vendors, products and packages you
run, so you hear about a new KEV listing or exploit without having to go
looking.

It runs on your own computer as a desktop app. There is no CVE Intel account
or server: lookups go straight from your machine to the public sources, and
the built-in AI assistant runs locally unless you choose a cloud provider.
The same program also works from the command line, as a REST API, and as an
MCP server for AI agents (see Developer notes). It is
built for security analysts, IT and operations teams, developers checking
their dependencies, and anyone learning vulnerability management.

### What it helps you do

- **Decide whether to patch now.** Enter a CVE ID and get a risk score from
 0 to 100, a plain recommendation and how urgent it is, with the evidence
 behind it.
- **Put a list of vulnerabilities in order.** Paste up to 10 CVE IDs from a
 scanner report and get the order to patch them in.
- **Check your project's dependencies.** Drop a project folder on the
 window, or paste a lockfile or SBOM. You see which packages have known
 vulnerabilities, ranked by how likely they are to hurt you (Log4Shell
 first, not just the highest CVSS), and which version fixes them. Scan
 again later to see what is new, fixed or riskier since last time.
- **Check what you run and ship.** Scan the apps and operating system on
 this computer, or a container image you build (no Docker needed). Or see
 what public sources already know about your own domains and servers,
 without CVE Intel ever connecting to them.
- **See what affects the products you run.** List the known vulnerabilities
 for a product and version, such as Apache Tomcat 9.0.80, with actively
 exploited ones first.
- **See what changed this week.** Open **Landscape** for new CISA KEV
 entries, CVEs ENISA marks exploited that KEV does not list yet, rising
 EPSS scores, new Metasploit modules and PoCs, new critical CVEs, Project
 Zero's in-the-wild zero-days and the latest CISA advisories. CVEs that
 several sources agree on are listed first.
- **Watch the products you run.** Add a vendor, product, package or CVE to
 the local watchlist. Each refresh records what changed: new CVEs, KEV
 listings, EPSS jumps, new exploits, CVSS revisions and newly available
 fixes.
- **Keep an eye on what attackers are exploiting.** Filter CISA's catalog of
 actively exploited vulnerabilities by vendor, product, ransomware use or
 date.
- **Investigate something suspicious.** Check an IP address from your logs,
 a file hash your antivirus flagged, or an unfamiliar domain or URL against
 threat-intelligence sources.
- **Ask questions in plain English.** *"Should we patch CVE-2024-3400 this
 weekend?"* The AI assistant looks up the facts first, then explains them,
 and shows which sources it used.
- **Give AI coding assistants the same knowledge.** Claude Code, Cursor, VS
 Code and other tools can use CVE Intel while they work, through MCP.

### Terms you'll see

| Term | What it means |
|---|---|
| **CVE** | A public ID for one known vulnerability, such as CVE-2021-44228 (Log4Shell). |
| **CVSS** | A 0–10 severity score: how bad the flaw is if someone exploits it. It says nothing about how likely an attack is. |
| **EPSS** | The probability that a vulnerability will be exploited in the next 30 days, published daily by FIRST. |
| **CISA KEV** | The US government's catalog of vulnerabilities known to be exploited by attackers. A CVE on this list is urgent. |
| **ENISA EUVD** | The EU vulnerability database. Its own "exploited" flag is independent of CISA KEV and can raise the SSVC Exploitation input. |
| **Exploit / PoC** | Public code that demonstrates or carries out an attack. A Metasploit module means the attack is packaged and easy to use. |
| **SSVC** | A decision method from CISA and CERT/CC that ends in one of four actions: *Act*, *Attend*, *Track\** or *Track*. |
| **SBOM / lockfile** | A list of every package your software uses, with exact versions. |
| **MCP** | Model Context Protocol, the standard way AI assistants call outside tools. |

The **risk score** combines these signals: severity (CVSS), the chance of
exploitation (EPSS), confirmed exploitation (CISA KEV) and public exploit
code. Anything on CISA KEV is always CRITICAL. See Risk score
for the formula.

> CVE Intel helps you decide what to patch. It does not probe, port-scan or
> attack anything, and it does not apply fixes. Scans read what is already
> on your machine (dependency files, the software installed on this
> computer, a container image you choose) and send only package and product
> names and versions to OSV.dev and NVD. The exposure check is passive: it
> asks public sources (Shodan, certificate transparency logs) what they
> already know about domains and addresses you own, and sends nothing to
> them. Results are only as current as the public sources.

## Getting started

You don't need an account or any API keys to start. Most people are
looking at their first result within a couple of minutes:

1. Download the app for your operating system and open it. The
 **Landscape** view loads first: what changed this week across the public
 sources.
2. Open **CVE Triage**, type a CVE ID such as `CVE-2024-3400` and press
 **Triage**, or click one of the examples under the search box. Press
 **Watch CVE** (or **Watch** next to the vendor) to be told when it
 changes.
3. Drag a project folder onto the window to check its dependencies, or open
 **Scan** and choose **This computer** to check the software installed on
 this machine. Findings come back ranked by real-world risk, with the
 version that fixes each one.
4. Press `⌘K` (`Ctrl+K` on Windows and Linux) to open **Quick Find**. Paste
 anything there (a CVE, IP address, file hash, domain, URL or
 `package:ecosystem:version`) and CVE Intel picks the right lookup.
5. *Optional:* in **Settings → Data source API keys**, add free API keys for
 faster lookups and more exploit data. See API keys.
6. *Optional:* open **Local Model** and download a model to use **Ask AI**
 with answers that never leave your computer.
7. *Optional:* open **MCP Server** to connect your AI coding assistant.

The buttons at the bottom of the sidebar switch between the light and dark
themes and make the text larger or smaller. The version you are running is
shown below them.

Everything up to Developer notes is about the desktop
app. To use CVE Intel from a terminal, a script, a CI pipeline or another
program, go straight to that section.

## Features

### Threat landscape

What changed recently, from several independent sources at once: new CISA
KEV entries (with ransomware flags and vendor counts), CVEs ENISA EUVD
marks exploited that CISA KEV does not list, the largest EPSS rises, new
or updated Metasploit modules and PoC-in-GitHub repositories, newly
published critical NVD CVEs, Project Zero's in-the-wild zero-days and the
latest CISA advisories. Each panel names its source and when it was
fetched, and the ⓘ on each tile explains what it counts. Your watchlist
comes first, then the CVEs that appear in two or more panels. Each watched
item is a chip that opens it in the **Watchlist**. Copy the
briefing as Markdown for a ticket or weekly note. Ask *"What's new this
week?"* in **Ask AI** for the same briefing.

Threat landscape for the last 7 days: tiles for watchlist changes, KEV additions, exploitation ENISA reports but KEV does not list, new exploits and PoCs, EPSS risers, new critical CVEs, this year's zero-days and CISA advisories, above the watchlist panel with a chip for each watched item and its latest changes, such as Palo Alto Networks and Ivanti CVEs added to CISA KEV

### Watchlist

Watch the vendors, products, packages and CVEs you run. Each refresh
compares them with the last check and records what changed: new CVEs, KEV
listings, ransomware use, EPSS jumps, new exploits or Metasploit modules,
CVSS changes, newly available fixes and ENISA exploitation reports. The
first check of an item records a silent baseline. The list lives only on
this machine (`~/.cve-intel/watch.db`, owner-only). While the app is open
it can refresh on a schedule (every 6 hours by default; change or turn it
off in **Settings**). AI agents can read the watchlist over MCP but cannot
change it.

Watchlist of Fortinet, Palo Alto Networks, Ivanti, Citrix, Apache Tomcat 9.0.80, lodash 4.17.20 and CVE-2024-3400, with what a refresh recorded: Palo Alto Networks, Ivanti and Fortinet CVEs added to CISA KEV in October, new KEV-listed CVEs for Fortinet and Citrix, and four EPSS jumps, one from 9.1% to 94.0%

### CVE Triage

One lookup across NVD, CVE.org, EPSS, CISA KEV, ENISA EUVD and public
exploit sources. The result includes the risk score, a plain recommendation
and urgency, and the evidence behind it: CVSS (and where it came from),
30-day EPSS probability and its recent trend, KEV dates, ENISA's exploited
flag, CIRCL sightings (deep triage), and the exploit evidence found in
Metasploit, Exploit-DB, Nuclei, GitHub, PoC-in-GitHub and, with a
VulnCheck token, VulnCheck KEV and XDB. When NVD has not scored a CVE yet,
the CNA's or CISA's score from the CVE.org record is used. Deep triage
also returns a CISA SSVC decision, using CISA's own published SSVC
assessment (Vulnrichment) where one exists. ENISA EUVD or VulnCheck KEV
can raise SSVC Exploitation to `active`; they do not change the risk
score.

The interface follows your system's light or dark theme until you pick one
with the sun and moon button at the bottom of the sidebar. Beside it,
**A−** and **A+** make the text and controls smaller or larger in every
view (`⌘ −`, `⌘ +` and `⌘ 0` on macOS; `Ctrl` on Windows and Linux), and
the size is remembered.

Deep CVE Triage for CVE-2024-3400 in the dark theme: a 100/100 CRITICAL score, CISA KEV and ENISA exploited flags, a weaponized exploit, CISA's SSVC "Act" decision, and the Metasploit and Exploit-DB entries for it

### Ask in plain language

Ask questions such as *"Which is worse: CVE-2024-3400 or CVE-2023-44487?"*
CVE Intel runs the right lookups first, then the model explains the results.
Each answer lists the tools it used, so you can check where the facts came from.
Small local models can still get details wrong, so check an answer you will
act on against **CVE Triage**.

### Compare and prioritise

Paste 2 to 10 CVE IDs to compare them and get a patch order based on KEV
status, score, EPSS and exploit evidence, not on CVSS alone. Not sure where
to start? The examples under the box (**KEV vs. CVSS**, **VPN & firewall
zero-days**, **Microsoft patch day** and **Open-source libraries**) each
show one way the order can surprise you.

CISA KEV CVEs come first, then the risk score. Equal scores are common
(exploited CVEs with a high EPSS all reach 100), so ties are broken by known
ransomware use, EPSS, exploit maturity, CVSS and the earlier KEV due date.
Each CVE says why it sits above the next one.

- **Side by side**: one column per CVE, with rows for the score's parts, KEV
 dates, ransomware use, who reports exploitation, EPSS and its 30-day trend,
 exploit sources, CVSS attack vector, complexity, privileges, user interaction
 and impact, product, CWE and age. Riskier values that differ are in red.
 **Only rows that differ** hides the rest.
- **What they have in common**: CVEs in the same product (one update may cover
 them) or from the same vendor, ransomware use, exploitation reported outside
 CISA KEV (which the score doesn't count), network access without sign-in or
 user action, public exploits, rising EPSS, and shared weaknesses.

Compare CVEs running the KEV vs. CVSS example: Log4Shell and HTTP/2 Rapid Reset, both in CISA KEV, ranked above curl's CVSS 9.8 SOCKS5 flaw, with the reason each one sits above the next

### Scan dependencies

Drop a project folder or dependency files anywhere on the window, or use
**Choose folder…** / **Choose files…**. A folder is searched, including
subfolders, for the lockfiles, manifests and SBOMs listed below. The search
skips `node_modules`, virtualenvs, `vendor`, build output and hidden
folders, and skips a `package.json` or `go.sum` that sits next to the
lockfile that pins it. Each file found is listed with its format and
package count. Untick any you don't want, then press **Scan**. Every file is
parsed on its own, a package listed in several files is checked once, and
each finding names the files it came from. Files are read on your machine;
only package names and versions are sent to OSV.dev.

You can also paste a lockfile (`package-lock.json`, `yarn.lock`, `Pipfile.lock`,
`poetry.lock`, `uv.lock`, `Cargo.lock`, `go.sum`, `go.mod`, `composer.lock`,
`Gemfile.lock`), an SBOM (CycloneDX JSON or XML, SPDX JSON or tag-value), a
`requirements.txt`, `package.json` or `pom.xml`, purls, or
`name:ecosystem:version` lines (for example from `apk info -v` or
`dpkg -l`; Alpine needs its release, as in `openssl:Alpine:v3.19:3.1.4-r0`).
The format is detected automatically and up to 10,000 packages are checked
against OSV.dev.

Findings are ranked by risk, not just severity. Each one gets the same
signals as **CVE Triage**: whether its CVE is in CISA KEV (and used by
ransomware), its EPSS score, exploit evidence from Exploit-DB and
Metasploit, and the risk score. Log4Shell in an old
`log4j-core` comes out on top; a CVSS 9.8 nobody exploits does not. When
GitHub, PyPI and a distribution each publish the same issue, it is shown
once. Filter by risk, KEV or whether a fix exists, or switch to **By
package** to see each vulnerable package with its advisories and the
version that fixes them. In a CI pipeline the same scan can fail the build
or feed GitHub code scanning; see CI and automation.

Scan of a demo project with four dependency files, findings ranked by risk: Log4Shell in log4j-core first, with CISA KEV, ransomware and weaponized-exploit signals, then HTTP/2 Rapid Reset in golang.org/x/net, a second Log4j flaw and Spring4Shell, each with the version that fixes it

Every scan is saved in **History**, on this computer only. Scan the same
folder again (or press **Scan again**) and the results say what changed
since the scan before: findings that are new, resolved (and whether an
upgrade or a removal fixed them), or riskier because they were added to
CISA KEV, gained an exploit or jumped in EPSS. A pasted list is saved under
a hash of its packages, never its text. **Copy as Markdown** puts the
findings table on the clipboard for a ticket, and **Forget** deletes every
scan of a target.

Scan History after the demo project was scanned again: log4j-core upgraded to 2.17.1 and lodash to 4.17.21 and ws added, so the row shows 3 new and 6 resolved findings, with the Monitor switch, Scan again and Forget, and each resolved CVE marked as fixed by an upgrade

**Watch all affected** adds the affected packages and apps of a scan to
the Watchlist, riskiest first, so you hear when one of them
is added to CISA KEV or gains an exploit. Tick **Monitor** next to a target
in History to have CVE Intel scan it again every day while the app is open
(the same folders, this computer, the same image or the same exposure
targets); what becomes new or riskier appears in the Watchlist feed and on
the Landscape.

### Scan this computer

**Scan → This computer** checks the operating system and the apps installed
on this machine. On Windows they come from the registry (the programs in
**Installed apps**, including per-user installs) and the Windows build; on
macOS from **Applications**, **~/Applications**, Homebrew (Apple silicon and
Intel) and the macOS version. **List installed software** shows what was
found and what will be checked, without contacting anything. **Check**
sends NVD only the vendor, product and version of the apps CVE Intel
recognises (browsers, Java, Acrobat, archivers, remote-access tools, VPN
clients, developer tools and about 100 more) and of the OS, then ranks the
findings like any other scan.

Apps CVE Intel does not recognise are listed as not checked, with the
reason. Tick **Also look up apps CVE Intel does not recognise** to ask NVD's
product dictionary for them: this sends their names to NVD, and a match is
kept only when NVD's vendor fits the app's publisher. Without an NVD API key
NVD allows a few requests a minute, so a first scan checks the riskiest
apps (browsers, Java, Acrobat, the OS) first and leaves the rest for the
next scan; answers are cached, so later scans are quicker. Programs that are
parts of others (system components, drivers) are skipped, and Microsoft 365
and the Visual C++ runtimes are reported as not checked because NVD lists
them without versions.

### Scan a container image

**Scan → Container image** checks a saved image without Docker: drop a
`docker save` or OCI archive (`.tar`, `.tar.gz`) on the window, or choose an
OCI layout folder. The image is read on your computer in one pass, layer by
layer, without unpacking anything to disk. Its operating system packages
(Debian, Ubuntu, Alpine, Wolfi, Chainguard, Red Hat, Rocky, AlmaLinux, Azure
Linux and openSUSE) and any lockfiles, manifests or SBOMs inside it are
checked with OSV.dev and ranked like any other scan. A multi-platform image
is scanned for this computer's architecture unless you name another
platform. Images whose distribution OSV does not cover (Fedora, Amazon
Linux, SUSE Linux Enterprise, Debian testing) and older rpm databases are
listed as not checked rather than reported clean.

```bash
docker save myapp:latest -o myapp.tar
cve-intel scan image myapp.tar --fail-on kev
```

### Check your public exposure

**Scan → Public exposure** shows what public sources already know about
domains and addresses you own. Enter domains or public IP addresses, confirm
they are yours (or that you are authorised to assess them), and press **Find
addresses**: CVE Intel collects host names from certificate transparency
logs (crt.sh, keeping only names under your domain), resolves them, and
lists the public addresses, dropping private and reserved ones. Untick any
that are not yours, then press **Check**. For each address it asks Shodan
(with a Shodan key) or the free Shodan InternetDB what services, software
versions and CVEs have been seen there, then checks the versions with NVD
and ranks the findings like any other scan.

The check is passive: CVE Intel never connects to the targets, and nothing
is port-scanned. Addresses that belong to a CDN or hosting platform are
flagged and left out, because the software seen there is the provider's.
CVEs Shodan infers from a banner are marked as reported, not verified, and
distribution builds (Ubuntu, Debian, RHEL) may have the fix backported.

```bash
cve-intel scan exposure example.com --authorized --list-only   # names and addresses only
cve-intel scan exposure example.com 203.0.113.10 --authorized --max-ips 20
```

### Databases and data sources

See every upstream source: what it provides, whether it needs a key, whether
your key is set, how long results are cached, and which tools use it. Press
**Check connectivity** to probe all of them live. The view also shows the
local cache, downloaded models and the model runtime.

Databases view: 39 upstream sources, 24 of them free without a key, the local cache and downloaded model, and a connectivity check with 29 of 39 sources reachable and 7 waiting on an API key

### MCP server for AI agents

Give AI agents CVE Intel's 38 tools while they work. Start the server from
the app, choose your agent, and copy setup steps with the correct address
and executable path already filled in. Guides are included for Claude Code,
Cursor, VS Code, Claude Desktop, Windsurf and any other MCP client.

- **Local only.** The server listens on `127.0.0.1` and refuses requests

## Local AI

**Ask AI** uses a small language model that runs on your computer, so your
questions stay private. Small models are poor at calling tools on their
own, so Ask works in three layers:

1. **Look up first.** Before the model runs, CVE Intel finds the CVE IDs,
 IPs, hashes and domains in your question, runs the matching lookups, and
 gives the results to the model as facts it must rely on.
2. **Explain the evidence.** The model explains those results and can ask
 for more lookups. It uses native llama.cpp tool calls, with a
 JSON-in-text fallback for very small models. If structured output fails,
 the question is retried as plain chat grounded in the same results.
3. **Works without a model.** If no model is running, Ask returns the
 lookup results directly, so the app is useful before any download
 finishes.

Open the **Local Model** view to install a runtime and download a model, one
click each. Every OS gets the official llama.cpp runtime, installed into
`~/.cve-intel/bin/`, with GGUF models in `~/.cve-intel/models/`. On a Mac
with Apple silicon (M1 or newer) the view also offers MLX, which runs
the model on the Mac's GPU and answers noticeably faster: one click installs
`mlx-lm` into a private Python environment in `~/.cve-intel/mlx/` (no
system Python needed), and MLX models download into `~/.cve-intel/models/`
too. Either model server runs on `127.0.0.1` only.

| Model | Runtime | Download | Min RAM | Notes |
|---|---|---:|---:|---|
| Qwen 2.5 1.5B Instruct (Q4_K_M) | llama.cpp | ~1.0 GB | 4 GB | Fastest |
| **Qwen 2.5 3B Instruct (Q4_K_M)** | llama.cpp | ~1.9 GB | 6 GB | Recommended default |
| Llama 3.2 1B Instruct (Q4_K_M) | llama.cpp | ~0.8 GB | 4 GB | Smallest |
| Llama 3.2 3B Instruct (Q4_K_M) | llama.cpp | ~2.0 GB | 6 GB | Strong chat |
| Qwen 2.5 7B Instruct (Q4_K_M) | llama.cpp | ~4.7 GB | 10 GB | Optional upgrade |
| Qwen 2.5 1.5B Instruct (MLX, 4-bit) | MLX | ~0.9 GB | 8 GB | Apple silicon only |
| Llama 3.2 1B Instruct (MLX, 4-bit) | MLX | ~0.7 GB | 8 GB | Apple silicon only; smallest and fastest |

MLX models are listed only on Macs that can run them. If you already have
`mlx-lm` (for example from Homebrew), CVE Intel uses it instead of
installing its own.

### Cloud providers (opt-in)

For stronger answers, open **Settings → AI provider**, choose OpenAI,
Anthropic or Google Gemini, pick a model and paste your API key. **Save &
use** enables the provider and tests the key. You can switch back to the
local model at any time.

| Provider | Default model | Environment variable |
|---|---|---|
| OpenAI | `gpt-4o` | `OPENAI_API_KEY` |
| Anthropic | `claude-sonnet-4-5` | `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` |

- **Off by default.** When a cloud provider is selected, each question and

 with tool calling. Anthropic describes its compatible endpoint as intended
 mainly for evaluation; for Claude-specific features, use CVE Intel through

| Vulnerability intelligence | NVD, NVD change history, CVE.org, CISA Vulnrichment, EPSS (FIRST) and its daily score files, CISA KEV, ENISA EUVD, VulnCheck NVD++, VulnCheck KEV, MSRC, Red Hat, Ubuntu |
| Exploit intelligence | GitHub PoC search, PoC-in-GitHub (nomi-sec), Exploit-DB, Metasploit modules, Nuclei templates, Project Zero 0day In the Wild |
| Network intelligence | AbuseIPDB, GreyNoise, Shodan, crt.sh, CIRCL Passive DNS |
| Threat intelligence | VirusTotal, MalwareBazaar, ThreatFox, URLScan, CISA advisories (RSS), CIRCL Vulnerability-Lookup sightings, Ransomwhere, CIRCL hashlookup |
| DevSecOps and reference | OSV.dev, GitHub Advisories, MITRE ATT&CK (STIX), CTID KEV → ATT&CK mappings, MITRE CAPEC, HIBP Pwned Passwords |

Many tools need no API key at all: EPSS and its daily files, KEV, ENISA
EUVD, CVE.org and CISA Vulnrichment, OSV, CVSS, Exploit-DB, Metasploit,
PoC-in-GitHub, Project Zero, CISA advisories, CIRCL sightings, ATT&CK,
CAPEC, crt.sh, Ransomwhere, hashlookup, Pwned Passwords, and NVD at a
lower rate limit. Large feeds (EPSS daily files, Exploit-DB, Metasploit,
ATT&CK, CAPEC, the CTID mappings) are downloaded once, reduced to a small
index, and refreshed daily or every few hours.

### Risk score

```
Risk = CVSS×0.20 + EPSS×0.35 + KEV×0.30 + PoC×0.15   (boosters up to ×1.27, capped at 100)
```

- **KEV override:** a CVE in CISA KEV is confirmed exploited, so it is always
 **CRITICAL** with a score of at least 76. Only CISA KEV earns the KEV
 points and the override.
- EPSS measures the probability of exploitation. CVSS is treated as severity,
 not likelihood.
- **PoC** is the strongest public exploit evidence. A Metasploit exploit
 module counts as weaponized (the full 15 points); Exploit-DB entries and
 VulnCheck XDB exploits count as public exploits.
- Deep triage also returns the **SSVC v2** CISA Deployer decision:
 `Act`, `Attend`, `Track*` or `Track`. Its inputs come from CISA's published
 SSVC assessment when there is one. Because that assessment is a snapshot,
 newer evidence can raise Exploitation: a CISA KEV, VulnCheck KEV or ENISA
 EUVD exploited listing, or an EPSS of 0.90 or more, makes it `active`.
 EUVD and VulnCheck do not change the risk score.
- Bands: 0–25 LOW, 26–50 MEDIUM, 51–75 HIGH, 76–100 CRITICAL.
- This is scoring version 1.1, reported as `scoring_version` in results.

## API keys

Keys are optional. Each one unlocks more data or raises a rate limit. In the
app, open **Settings → Data source API keys**, press **Get a key** to open
the sign-up page, paste the key and press **Save**. The key is used on the
next lookup, with no restart needed.

| Key | What it unlocks | Get it |
|---|---|---|
| NVD API key | 10× faster CVE lookups | nvd.nist.gov |
| GitHub token (no scopes) | Exploit search, Nuclei templates and advisory fixed versions (5,000 instead of 60 requests/hour) | github.com/settings/tokens |
| VulnCheck token | VulnCheck KEV (exploitation reports and XDB exploit links), and backup CVE data if NVD is down | vulncheck.com |
| AbuseIPDB key | IP abuse score | abuseipdb.com |
| GreyNoise key | Whether an IP is harmless background noise | docs.greynoise.io |
| Shodan key | Open ports and services on an IP | account.shodan.io |
| VirusTotal key | 70+ antivirus verdicts for a file hash | virustotal.com |
| URLScan key | Higher limits for URL checks | urlscan.io |
| abuse.ch Auth-Key | MalwareBazaar and ThreatFox lookups | auth.abuse.ch |
| CIRCL passive DNS login | Historical DNS records (access by request) | circl.lu |

Keys are stored in `~/.cve-intel/settings.db` with owner-only permissions
and shared by the app, CLI, MCP server and REST API on the same machine. A
key saved in the app takes precedence over an environment variable. Free
tiers and sign-up steps are set by each vendor, so check their pages. To
manage keys from a terminal or with environment variables, see
Terminal configuration.

## Privacy and security

- All network traffic is outbound HTTPS: to the data sources, to the cloud
 AI provider if you opt in to one, and for the model and runtime
 downloads you start (Hugging Face, the llama.cpp release on GitHub and,
 for MLX, `uv` and a Python 3.12 build from GitHub plus `mlx-lm` from
 PyPI).
- API keys are never logged, cached, shown in the UI or returned by any tool.
- Private and reserved IPs are rejected before any network lookup.
- The local model server and the app's MCP server bind to loopback only.
- SQLite files are created on first use: `cache.db`, a disposable lookup
 cache; `~/.cve-intel/settings.db`, which holds keys, provider settings
 and the watchlist auto-refresh interval; and `~/.cve-intel/watch.db`,
 the local watchlist (items, snapshots and change events). Clearing the
 cache never touches settings or the watchlist.
- While the app is open, an optional background task can refresh the
 watchlist (every 6 hours by default). It only contacts the public
 sources needed for the items you watch, and you can turn it off in
 **Settings**. Nothing runs while the app is closed.
- The desktop app keeps an activity log in `~/.cve-intel/activity.db`
 (owner-only). It records what you look up and ask, the answers, setting
 and model changes, the tools agents call through the app's MCP server, and
 which hosts each action contacted. API keys are never recorded, only key
 names. Upstream requests are stored as host and path, without query
 strings. Open **Activity** to search it, pause it or clear it. It keeps
 the latest 20,000 entries. The CLI and `cve-intel mcp` record nothing.

See SECURITY.md for the full security model and how to report
a vulnerability.

## Developer notes

Everything in this section is for using CVE Intel from a terminal, scripts,
CI pipelines, other programs or AI agents, and for building it yourself. The
desktop app needs none of it.

- The `cve-intel` executable: where it is and how one file runs every mode
- Command line (CLI): every command, with recipes for common tasks
- CI and automation: fail a build, upload SARIF to GitHub code scanning, JSON output
- REST API: endpoints and examples
- MCP server setup: connect AI agents by hand
- Terminal configuration: keys, environment variables, your own model server
- Build from source and Docker
- Architecture and Development and tests

### The `cve-intel` executable

The desktop app and the command-line tool are the same file. Double-clicking
it opens the app; running it with any argument starts the CLI, the MCP
server or the REST server instead.

| OS | Executable |
|---|---|
| macOS | `/Applications/CVE Intel.app/Contents/MacOS/cve-intel` |
| Windows (default per-user install) | `%LOCALAPPDATA%\CVE Intel\cve-intel.exe` |
| Linux | `/usr/bin/cve-intel` (`.deb`), or the downloaded `.AppImage` |

```bash
# macOS
"/Applications/CVE Intel.app/Contents/MacOS/cve-intel" triage CVE-2024-3400
# Linux
./CVE-Intel_<version>_linux-x64.AppImage triage CVE-2024-3400
# Windows (default per-user install)
"%LOCALAPPDATA%\CVE Intel\cve-intel.exe" triage CVE-2024-3400
```

> On Windows the executable is a windowed program, so the terminal does not
> wait for it. To see the output in order, use
> `start /wait "" "…\cve-intel.exe" triage CVE-2024-3400`, or in PowerShell
> `& "…\cve-intel.exe" … | Out-Host`. MCP clients start it directly and are
> not affected.

For servers and containers there is also a headless build without the GUI
(`cargo build --release -p cve-server`, which produces
`target/release/cve-intel`). From a source checkout, replace `cve-intel`
with `cargo run -p cve-server --`. The examples below assume `cve-intel` is
on your `PATH`.

### Command line (CLI)

```bash
cve-intel triage CVE-2024-3400 --depth deep
cve-intel ask "Should we patch CVE-2021-44228?" --model qwen2.5-3b
cve-intel quick-find 185.220.101.34
cve-intel scan deps .                          # every lockfile, manifest and SBOM here, ranked by risk
cve-intel scan deps . --fail-on kev            # exit 3 if anything is in CISA KEV
cve-intel fix lodash npm 4.17.15               # version that fixes every known vulnerability
cve-intel product confluence_data_center --vendor atlassian --version 8.5.0
cve-intel kev-search --vendor microsoft --ransomware-only --epss
cve-intel landscape --days 7                    # what

title: Show HN: Panel – A research workspace where the agent can build its own panes
author: greentfrapp

# greentfrapp/panel

- Stars: 78
- Forks: 7
- Watchers: 78
- Open issues: 0
- License: MIT License
- Default branch: main
- Created: 2026-09-15T06:18:47Z

## Languages

- CSS
- HTML
- JavaScript
- Python
- TypeScript
- Vue

## Top Contributors

- greentfrapp (594 contributions)

---

## README

# Panel

A research workspace where the agent works beside you: chat, files, PDFs and notebooks in one dock, and the agent can also create custom viewers and apps when necessary

This is an early build for testers. Expect rough edges, and feel free to raise issues.

Screenshot of Panel in action.

## Before you start

- Node 22.18 or newer (or 24.12 and newer)
- pnpm
- uv, which fetches the Python it needs (3.12 or newer) by itself
- Claude Code, installed and signed in: run `claude` once and log in. The agent and the literature review run through it.

## Install and start

```sh
pnpm install
uv sync
pnpm start
```

Then open. `pnpm start` builds the app first, so the first start takes a minute. Ctrl-C stops everything it started.

## Where your things are

- `~/Panel/panel.db` holds your conversations and everything the agents did.
- `~/Panel/workspaces` is where new Workspaces are created, unless you pick another folder.

Both are outside this folder, so deleting or re-cloning the repo keeps them.

## What works

- Chatting with an agent that can read and write files, and asks before running a tool.
- Workspaces: a folder the agent works in, with its own chats and saved layout.
- Panes for files, PDFs, markdown and Jupyter notebooks. Notebooks run against a real kernel, and you and the agent can edit the same one.
- Long-running commands in the background, which you can watch and stop.
- Panes the agent writes for you when you ask to see something a built-in Pane cannot show.
- A literature review: ask the chat for one, and open its result from the tool card.

## What doesn't yet

- Currently only has full support for Claude Code.
- Modules start only by asking the chat. There is no button to launch one.
- The hypothesis Modules have no view of their own, so their results can be hard to read.
- Modules don't work with OpenAI API yet.

## The OpenAI key (optional)

Copy `apps/server/.env.example` to `apps/server/.env` and set `OPENAI_API_KEY`. This adds "OpenAI API" to the agent picker, for chat and tools.

It does not run literature reviews or the hypothesis Modules: those need an agent that can search the web, and today only Claude Code can. Without a key, the picker shows OpenAI as not set up, which is expected.

## If something's wrong

- **"Panel couldn't reach its server."** The server half is not running. Check the terminal `pnpm start` is in, then press Retry.
- **An agent shows as not set up.** The reason is written under the message box.
- **A port is already in use**, or the app answers but never loads: run `pnpm dev:doctor`. It says what is holding each port and how to clear it.

## Licence

MIT

---

## The idea

### UI

The UI has multiple configurable windows, called Panes, that can display things ranging from image files, data files, code, as well as chat sessions. This is critical for researchers who often have to context switch between different types of files.

A default set of Panes are provided for common use cases. But custom Panes can also be added by humans and agents, such as a PDB viewer or SQLite visualizer.

### Module Protocol

Modules are similar to Skills but with additional definitions to support inter-module workflows and integration with the workspace.

Specifically, Modules have typed definitions for Inputs, Outputs, and Intermediates.

Inputs and Outputs are straightforward. Intermediates refer to objects that provide observability, such as the Chain-of-Thought or scratchpad for an agentic Module, or may be intermediate outputs in a multi-stage Module. These are especially important for processes that need transparency or long-running jobs that should show progress.

Having typed definitions for these enable validation at runtime and make it easier for humans and agents to develop custom Modules for downstream tasks and Panes for visualizations.

#### Data Abstraction Layer

A data abstraction layer (DAL) bridges in-memory and filesystem objects. A DAL helps to map a URI to either an in-memory store or a local file, so that the Module just has to concern itself with the manipulation of the object.


# Lume — open-source terminal: command blocks, AI, remote control

# stagas/livediff

A live Git diff view cli

- Stars: 9
- Forks: 0

## Languages

- Shell

## Top Contributors

- stagas (2 contributions)

---

## README

# livediff

Stay on top of what your coding agents are doing with a live diff feed, right in
your terminal.

`livediff` watches the current Git repository and shows every edit as it happens,
whether it comes from an agent, an editor, or another tool. Changes appear like a
regular Git diff: added lines are green, removed lines are red, and unchanged
lines provide context. Each edit is shown once, keeping the feed focused on what
your agents are changing now.

## Install

Run this in your terminal:

```sh
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/stagas/livediff/main/install.sh | sh
```

The installer supports Linux and macOS on x64 or ARM64, and Windows x64 through
Git Bash. It downloads a standalone executable; only Git needs to be installed.

## Get started

Open a terminal in any Git repository and run:

```sh
livediff
```

Now edit and save a file. You will see output similar to:

```diff
diff --git a/example.ts b/example.ts 3:47:12 PM
--- a/example.ts
+++ b/example.ts
@@ -1,3 +1,3 @@
-const greeting = "Hello";
+const greeting = "Hello, world!";
```

Only edits made after `livediff` starts are displayed. It watches tracked files
and new files that are not excluded by your Git ignore rules.

Press `q` or Ctrl-C to stop.

## Compact mode

For a quieter view with only the filename, time, and changed lines, run:

```sh
livediff --compact
```

The short form works too:

```sh
livediff -c
```

Compact output looks like this:

```diff
example.ts 3:47:12 PM
-const greeting = "Hello";
+const greeting = "Hello, world!";
```

## Color and install location

Disable colors when redirecting output or using a terminal without color support:

```sh
NO_COLOR=1 livediff
```

The installer uses `/usr/local/bin` when it is writable and `~/.local/bin`
otherwise. To choose a different directory:

```sh
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/stagas/livediff/main/install.sh | INSTALL_DIR="$HOME/bin" sh
```

Release checksums are available as `SHA256SUMS` on the GitHub Releases page.

## Development

The project uses Go. To test or compile it from source:

```sh
go test ./...
go build -o dist/livediff .
```

## License

MIT © 2026 stagas

title: Show HN: Ordewell – turn one goal into an ordered plan of coding-agent tasks
author: ac-ciano
body:
# ordewell/ordewell

Multi-agent task orchestration for coding agents. Turn one goal into an ordered plan of tasks — each with its own runner, model and mode — then execute and verify the results.

- Stars: 4
- Forks: 0
- Watchers: 4
- Open issues: 0
- License: Other
- Default branch: main
- Created: 2026-07-31T15:20:40Z

## Languages

- CSS
- HTML
- JavaScript
- Shell
- TypeScript

## Top Contributors

- ac-ciano (10 contributions)

---

## README

 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 Turn one goal into an ordered plan of coding-agent tasks — each with its own runner, model and mode — then execute and verify it. 
 

 
 Website ·
 Docs 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

---

## What this is

- **A plan you can rewrite before a token is spent.** The plan is a typed artifact, not an agent's internal state: every task carries a runner, model, thinking effort and mode, and you can change any of them, add and remove tasks, and rewire dependencies — without losing completed work or round-tripping the AI.
- **The right model per task, chosen in the open.** The planner makes one portfolio decision across the whole plan — a security refactor and a README update do not deserve the same model — and shows you every assignment before anything runs (why a separate planner?).
- **Verdicts from evidence, not opinion.** A task completes only when its unique completion marker appears in the runner's output; exit code is retained as diagnostic evidence. The model is never the tie-breaker. Stuck tasks can be advanced with *Mark complete*, and a task marked done by mistake goes back with *Mark not done*.
- **A planner that talks back.** Planning is one continuous chat: it researches your repo read-only, asks when your goal is vague, and its final message *is* the plan (ADR-0002). Reads run in parallel; anything reaching outside the workspace asks once; commands that would write are refused outright (ADR-0008).
- **No extra API key required.** Claude Code, Codex, or OpenCode can *be* the planner, strictly read-only, on the subscription you already hold for the runners (ADR-0009).
- **Multi-runner by design.** Enable several and the planner assigns one per task. Claude Code, Codex and OpenCode ship built-in; anything else — Aider, your own CLI — is a plugin manifest, not a code change.

---

## Quick Start

Node.js ≥ 20 on macOS, Linux or Windows. The TUI also needs **tmux** — see
Platform support below.

```bash
npm install -g ordewell
ordewell                                       # the TUI — chat on the left, plan on the right
```

That's it. First run asks for a planner and a runner, set from inside
(`/planner`, `/runners`, `/key`) — no restart, no API key required up front.

`npx ordewell` works the same without a global install; the package also
ships scoped as `@ordewell/cli`.

For VS Code instead, install the extension — it carries its own core, so
there is nothing to install from npm:

```bash
code --install-extension ordewell.ordewell
```

Or search **Ordewell** in the Extensions view.

Building from source:
`git clone https://github.com/ordewell/ordewell.git && cd ordewell && npm install && npm run build && npm link -w packages/cli`
— see CONTRIBUTING.md.

### Scriptable / headless

Every slash command is also a subcommand — set the planner and runner by env
var to skip the TUI entirely.

**Already run Claude Code, Codex, or OpenCode?** No separate API key — it
runs on the subscription you already hold:

```bash
export AI_PROVIDER="claude-code"        # or codex, opencode
ordewell plan --goal "Add rate limiting to the public API" && ordewell run
```

Mutation always stays with the runners; the planner agent only explores and
reasons. Same toggles apply from a UI: `/planner`, `/model`,
`/planner-effort`, or the planner bar in VS Code.

**Prefer an API key?** Twenty-five providers are recognised via their own
`*_API_KEY` — OpenRouter, Anthropic, OpenAI, Gemini, xAI, Groq, DeepSeek,
Mistral, Together, Fireworks, Perplexity, Cerebras, DeepInfra, Cohere,
Novita, Kimi, Zhipu, Qwen, Doubao, Hunyuan, Baichuan, MiniMax, Yi, StepFun
and SiliconFlow. Run `ordewell key` for variable names, or point
`OPENAI_COMPATIBLE_BASE_URL` at anything else, including a local model
server.

```bash
export OPENROUTER_API_KEY="sk-or-..."
ordewell plan --goal "Add rate limiting to the public API" && ordewell run
```

---

## Three surfaces, one core

### VS Code

A streaming timeline: live thinking, each research step with its outcome, and task cards you expand for the runner's own output. Retarget a task's runner and its model and mode re-derive in place. The whole loop is below, under **The VS Code loop, end to end**.

### Terminal UI

 

Everything the extension does, over SSH. `tab` swaps chat and plan pane; single keys drive the plan (`f` start, `E` run all, `m` toggle done, `R` runner, `o` model). `/help` lists the rest.

### CLI

```console
$ ordewell plan --goal "Add rate limiting to the public API"

Generating plan for: "Add rate limiting to the public API"...
✓ list_dir src → D middleware F router.ts F auth.ts
✓ grep X-RateLimit → no matches in 6 files

Question: should limits apply per API key, or per client IP?
My recommendation: per key — auth() already threads the key through req.ctx.
> per key, with an IP fallback for anonymous routes

Plan: 4 tasks (3 AI, 1 Manual) — claude-code, opencode
Session: session-1751600000000

   1. [ AI] Add a token-bucket limiter in src/middleware/rateLimit.ts (Claude Sonnet 4.5 · Claude Code)
   2. [ AI] Wire the limiter into route registration (Claude Haiku 4.5 · Claude Code)
   3. [ AI] Return RFC 6585 429s with Retry-After (DeepSeek V4 Flash · Opencode)
   4. [MAN] Document the limit headers in the OpenAPI spec

  [MAN] = manual step — run `ordewell tui` to work through it

  Run 'ordewell run' to execute, 'ordewell status' to inspect, or 'ordewell tui' for the full UI.

$ ordewell run
Executing plan...
  ✓ #a1b2 completed — PASS: Verified: completion marker detected in agent output. Task c
  ⟳ #c3d4 in_progress
[2/Wire the limiter into route registration] Started: claude-code / claude-haiku-4-5

Done. 4 completed, 0 failed, 0 blocked.
```

Every slash command is also an `ordewell` subcommand, so nothing is UI-only and headless automation reaches everything a human can.

---

## How it works

1. **Describe a goal** in plain prose.
2. **The planner researches** your workspace read-only and interleaves questions with research in one persistent conversation (ADR-0008).
3. **A plan appears** — ordered tasks, each with a runner, model, thinking effort and mode. Edit anything inline, or reprompt to reshape the whole plan without losing completed work.
4. **Execution** spawns a real coding-agent session per AI task, respecting the dependency graph and handing each task its predecessors' results. Manual tasks become checklists.
5. **The VerdictEngine** completes a task only once its marker appears; an exit without one fails visibly. Sessions auto-save to `.ordewell/sessions/`.

---

 
 Usage examples — planning, editing, multi-runner, plugins 

**Plan, edit, execute**

```bash
# The planner researches the repo and converses if the goal is underspecified
ordewell plan --goal "Migrate the config loader from JSON to TOML"

# Reassign before running — runner first, since it re-derives model, effort and mode
ordewell task-runner 2 opencode
ordewell task-deps 3 1,2

# Execute; independent tasks run in parallel (default: 3 concurrent sessions)
ordewell run

# Inspect any session later
ordewell status --session-id session-1751600000000
```

The surfaces differ only in how you name a target: the TUI opens a picker, the CLI takes an argument — and omitting the argument prints the same options the picker would have shown.

```bash
ordewell task-model 3            # lists the models that task's runner can spawn
ordewell task-model 3 sonnet     # picks one
```

**Configure without an editor**

```bash
ordewell planner claude-code     # plan on a coding agent's subscription — no API key
ordewell model set sonnet        # scoped to that agent's own catalog
ordewell planner-effort high     # a variant of the selected model
ordewell key set openrouter sk-… # stored in .env, never echoed back
ordewell runners codex off
```

Each pushes to the running server *before* writing `.env`, so the change lands on the next plan with no restart — and a refused connection cannot leave the file holding a setting the daemon never saw.

**Deep-interview planning with a PRD**

```bash
ordewell grill-me on   # planner interrogates your goal before outlining (min. 3 probing questions)
ordewell prd on        # planner previews, then writes a full PRD to .scratch/<slug>/PRD.md
ordewell tdd on        # tasks are augmented with red-green-refactor instructions

ordewell plan --goal "Real-time collaborative editing"
# → the planner grills you in chat, drafts the PRD, waits for your OK,
#   then commits the plan as its final message
```

**Multi-runner plans and custom runners**

```bash
# Pass --runner repeatedly to build a runner set; the planner assigns one per task
ordewell plan --goal "Refactor auth module" --runner claude-code --runner opencode

# Bring your own CLI agent via a plugin manifest
ordewell plugins create my-runner        # scaffolds manifest.json
ordewell plugins install github:user/repo
ordewell plugins list
```

**The other two front ends**

```bash
ordewell               # full-screen terminal UI — same as `ordewell tui`
ordewell web --daemon  # the local API server, in the background
```

`ordewell web` starts the HTTP + WebSocket API on `127.0.0.1:3742` that the CLI and TUI are clients of — every other command starts it for you on demand. It serves JSON, not a web page; there is no browser dashboard yet.

For VS Code, install the extension and open the Ordewell panel — see Quick Start.

| Area | Commands |
| --- | --- |
| Planning | type a goal, `/approve`, `/run`, `/stop` |
| Tasks | `/add-task`, `/remove-task`, `/complete`, `/uncomplete`, `/skip`, `/retry`, `/cancel`, `/force-start` |
| Skills | `/grill-me`, `/tdd`, `/prd`, `/review`, `/verify`, `/research-subagents` |
| Models | `/model`, `/key`, `/allowlist`, `/runners`, `/auto`, `/refresh` |
| Sessions | `/sessions`, `/new`, `/save`, `/load`, `/delete` — a loaded session is adopted by the server, so its plan stays executable |
| System | `/help`, `/mouse`, `/quit` |

API keys typed into `/key` are masked on screen and written to your `.env`.

Text is selectable and copyable with the mouse, as in any other program: Ordewell
does not capture the terminal's mouse. Scroll with `pgup`/`pgdn`. If you would
rather have wheel scrolling and can live without drag-to-select, `/mouse on`
swaps the trade (and remembers it via `ORDEWELL_TUI_MOUSE` in your `.env`).

A task's own terminal is a tmux window, where tmux does hold the mouse so the
wheel scrolls its scrollback. Selecting there still copies to your system
clipboard: drag to select and release to copy, or double/triple-click for a word
or a line. Install `wl-copy`, `xclip` or `xsel` on Linux if you have none of them
— without one, copying falls back to an OSC 52 escape that some terminals ignore.

 

 
 The VS Code loop, end to end — research, question, plan, execution, verdict 

 

 

 
 Platform support — including the Windows notes 

| Surface | Linux | macOS | Windows |
|---------|-------|-------|---------|
| VS Code extension | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| API server | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| CLI | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| TUI | ✅ needs tmux | ✅ needs tmux | needs tmux — run it under WSL |

**The TUI requires tmux on every platform**, not only Windows — it is what backs
each task's live terminal. Install it from your package manager (`apt install
tmux`, `brew install tmux`) before running `ordewell`. Everything else runs
natively on Windows: the planner (including harness planners), task execution,
model discovery, and the read-only exploration envelope all work there.

Two notes for Windows. Install the agent CLIs with their **native installers** where one exists — an npm-installed `claude`/`codex`/`opencode` is a `.cmd` shim, which has to start through cmd.exe and inherits its 8191-character command-line limit; that is fine for task prompts but not for the harness planner's larger system prompt, and Ordewell will tell you so by name rather than silently truncating it. And keep **Git for Windows** installed: its POSIX shell is what the planner runs research commands in, so `ls`, `cat`, `grep` and friends behave the same as they do everywhere else. See ADR-0010.

Any install route is found, on PATH or not: the PowerShell one-liner installers (`irm https://claude.ai/install.ps1 | iex`, OpenCode's equivalent), npm, pnpm, Yarn, bun, Scoop, Chocolatey, WinGet, and Volta. If a runner is greyed out in the picker right after you installed it, restart the VS Code window — a GUI-launched extension host holds the PATH it started with.

 

 
 Configuration — the four settings that matter 

| Option | Default | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| One provider key (`OPENROUTER_API_KEY`, `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, `GEMINI_API_KEY`, …) | — | The one required setting. Twenty-five providers are recognised, each from its own variable — `ordewell key` lists them — plus any OpenAI-compatible endpoint via `OPENAI_COMPATIBLE_BASE_URL`. The provider is auto-detected from whichever key is set (force with `AI_PROVIDER`). Not needed when `AI_PROVIDER` is `claude-code`, `codex`, or `opencode` — those plan with the CLI's own subscription. |
| `ORCHESTRATOR_MODEL` | `deepseek/deepseek-v4-flash` | The planner model — a budget model by default; it plans and researches but never writes code. Change via `ordewell model set ` or `/model`, which scope the choice to the planner backend's own catalog. With a coding-agent planner, it must be one of that agent's own model ids. |
| `ORDEWELL_PLANNER_EFFORT` | — | Thinking effort for a coding-agent planner, from the selected model's own variants (`low`, `high`, `adaptive`, …). Ignored by vendor planners, whose effort is baked into the model id. Change via `ordewell planner-effort ` or `/planner-effort`. |
| `ORDEWELL_MAX_PARALLEL` | `3` | Max concurrent AI task sessions (1–5). Independent tasks run in parallel; the dependency graph is always respected. |

Run `ordewell --help` for the full list of environment variables, or `ordewell setup` for the interactive wizard. VS Code users: everything is mirrored under `ordewell.*` settings.

 

 
 Architecture 

```text
packages/
├── core/    Pure TypeScript, zero UI deps — Session, PlanStore, Planner,
│            TaskOrchestrator, VerdictEngine, ModelResolver, ModeResolver,
│            RunnerRegistry + manifest template engine
├── cli/     ordewell: tui, plan, run, status, stop, web, models, setup,
│            plugins, grill-me, prd, tdd — plus tui/, a pure state +
│            renderer core behind a thin raw-mode terminal driver
├── vscode/  Extension + webview: streaming planner timeline, task cards,
│            TTY capture via script(1)
└── web/     Hono HTTP + WebSocket server — the local daemon the CLI and
             TUI drive over 127.0.0.1 (session pool, headless execution)
```

The TUI's core is pure — a reducer returning `{ state, effects }` and a renderer returning one string per terminal row (ADR-0006).

Tasks default to each runner's autonomous mode (toggle with `/auto`), and the plan is the source of truth for what runs — modes are never silently rewritten at spawn (ADR-0001).

Every surface consumes one event union (`SessionMessage`) over one broadcast seam — the domain vocabulary lives in CONTEXT.md and design decisions in docs/adr/.

 

 
 Acknowledgements 

The deep-interview planning workflows — `grill-me`, PRD drafting, TDD task augmentation, and review mode — are adapted from Matt Pocock's skills (MIT), rebuilt as prompt blocks inside Ordewell's planner and runner prompts. If you want those workflows in a plain coding-agent session rather than an orchestrated plan, his repo is the place to start.

 

---

## Contributing

Bug reports, feature requests and pull requests are welcome — start with CONTRIBUTING.md for the build order and the layout of the tree. Security issues go to SECURITY.md, not the public tracker.

New to the codebase? CONTEXT.md is the domain glossary and docs/adr/ records why things are the way they are.

## License

Licensed under the Apache License 2.0. The Ordewell name and logos are not covered by that licence — see NOTICE.

title: Show HN: An e-ink frame that hears birds and draws them as 1800s illustrations
author: arnemunthekaas
body:
# arnegiacomo/fugleramme

E-ink bird frame for Raspberry Pi - real-time bird detection by audio using BirdNET-Go

- Stars: 0
- Forks: 0
- Watchers: 0
- Open issues: 5
- License: MIT License
- Default branch: main
- Created: 2026-07-08T19:01:49Z

## Languages

- Python
- Shell

## Topics

- bird-detection
- birding
- birdnet
- birdnet-go
- birdwatching
- e-ink
- inky-impression
- kiosk-software
- machine-learning
- raspberry-pi

## Top Contributors

- arnegiacomo (46 contributions)

---

## README

# fugleramme
E-ink bird frame for Raspberry Pi - real-time bird detection by audio.

Built on top of BirdNET-Go, which runs
the mic and the BirdNET classifier and owns all detection config. Fugleramme reads
its detections and renders the recently-seen birds as a collage on an Inky-Impression e-ink panel, and serves the same view as a web kiosk.

## Art

The birds are cut-outs from historic, public-domain natural-history drawings,
hand-curated for this project. Each detected species is matched to its
illustration, background-removed, and packed onto a textured paper page - larger
birds toward the centre, sized by real body mass. Species with no illustration
are currently left off, and an empty window shows a bare perch.

| No detections | A few visitors | A full garden |
| :---: | :---: | :---: |
| No birds detected | A few garden birds | Many garden birds |

## Run locally

```bash
uv sync                                       # set up venv
uv run python -m fugleramme.seed --count 40   # seed db (no BirdNET-Go in dev)
uv run fugleramme-frame                       # start service on :8080
uv run fugleramme-dev                         # same as above with hot-reload
```

Open the kiosk (no SPI-panel needed):

```bash
open -na "Google Chrome" --args --kiosk --app=http://localhost:8080/
```

## Run on a Raspberry Pi

Clone the repo on the Pi and run the idempotent one-command bootstrap:

```bash
./setup.sh          # add -y to auto-accept dependency installs (uv, docker, etc...)
```

It installs any missing deps, brings up BirdNET-Go (container + mic), and enables
the frame as a systemd service that pushes to the Inky panel and serves the kiosk
on `:8080`. Details: `detector/README.md`. 

Want to update? Just pull and run ./setup.sh again

## License

- Code (`wikimedia-scrape/`, application code): MIT - see `LICENSE`.
- Bird images (`assets/birds/`): CC BY-SA 4.0 - see
 `assets/birds/ATTRIBUTION.md`.
- Bird sizes (`assets/bird_sizes.csv`): body mass from AVONET (Tobias et al.
 2022, Ecology Letters, doi:10.1111/ele.13898),
 CC BY 4.0.

comments.author: arnemunthekaas
comments.text: Author here. A mic listens to the sounds in my garden, BirdNET-Go (an open-source BirdNET classifier) detects birds by sound, and the e-ink frame draws a real 1800s natural-history illustration of each one as it hears them. Here’s a live web-demo from my garden in Bergen, Norway: https://fugleramme.arnegiacomo.devA few things that might be interesting:- The screen only redraws when the set of birds changes, and dithers the collage down to six colours for the e-ink display.- Bigger birds sit toward the centre, scaled by real body mass.- 800+ cutouts across 400+ species, each cut from a real public domain plate. All art is historic and human-made. Coverage is currently best for the Nordics, Britain and Germany (but other parts of the world are in the works).- Runs fully local on a Raspberry Pi or your homelab (yes, even the classifier runs great on a RPI)The e-ink panel is optional and it can run web-only in a container against a BirdNET-Go you already have.Happy to answer any questions!

comments.author: arnemunthekaas
comments.text:
Author here: Fair, i could've been more explicit in my writing. Concretely:Every bird is a cutout from a real scanned 1800s plate (Gould, the von Wright
brothers, Dresser...). The manifest (https://github.com/arnegiacomo/fugleramme/blob/main/assets/a...) links to each source, so you can compare them to the original scans. No bird has been prompt/diffusion generated, although I did use diffusion-based tools to remove birds from the perches (https://github.com/arnegiacomo/fugleramme/tree/main/assets/a...).Nothing at runtime uses AI either, at least in the sense of LLMs or diffusion. The collage is Pillow and numpy, and detection is BirdNET, which is a classifier, not a generative model.However I have used LLMs for code-related work, and for writing scripts for programatically editing the images, like cutting, contrast and colour corrections.

comments.author: originalvichy
comments.text: What do you mean specifically? These birdsong analyzers are sensitive enough that they do not rely on setting up a feeder. It’s obviously dependent on where you live, but in the Nordics, living outside city centres is good enough for both background noise and birdsong from nearby trees/parks/forests. Privacy matters aside, setting a mic up on a balcony or window is enough. Another solution is feeding data from a cheap security camera with a mic through wifi. This way the camera can stay outside in different weather, it’s not super close to you actual living area and splitting audio from the RTSP stream should be relatively easy to be analyzed by BirdNET.

comments.author: eichin
comments.text: Sounds like you've got birds crashing into the door? That's often something that can be improved (with stickers or hanging decorations) that make the glass more perceptible to the birds. (Another thing that sometimes helps is having bushes or shrubs, or even potted plants, in sight of the feeder - most small birds will use a "staging area" and fly somewhere nearby first, "check out the scene", and then fly to the feeder from there; it doesn't really control the activity, but it adds some options.)

comments.author: lambda
comments.text: There are LLMs that support audio input, similar to those with vision support.From my testing of open weights LLMs with audio support, they basically are only trained to recognize audio as an alternative to text input, they treat audio as basically equivalent to a transcript, and can't recognize or distinguish things like music, accents, background sounds, etc.So they're only really good for transcribing or summarizing or using audio input in place of text input for prompts, but not anything that requires distinguishing any information about the audio that would not be present in a transcript.It can be tempting to try to use an LLM for a variety of tasks; kind of the whole thing about an LLM is that you don't have to do a separate complex training run for every task, but can just provide instructions in natural language. But it only works as far as what the training data covers, if the training basically always treated audio and a text transcript as equivalent, the model has nothing causing it to learn other relevant features of the audio. If there's enough bird call identification in the training data of an LLM, it might be able to do that, but I think multimodal training data tends to be much more limited than the text training corpus

title: Show HN: Breathe CLI – Paced resonance breathing in the macOS terminal
author: marekkowalczyk
body: I built a terminal app that paces slow breathing at 6 breaths per minute for vagal tone training. It's a single Python file, stdlib only, no dependencies — just run breathe and follow the bar.I'm a cardiology patient (HFrEF). Slow breathing at resonance frequency is one of the few non-pharmacological interventions shown to improve cardiac vagal tone and baroreflex sensitivity (Bernardi et al., Circulation 2002; Lancet 1998). I wanted a frictionless daily habit tool — no app store, no account, no subscription, just open terminal and go.Design constraints, all grounded in the clinical literature:- No breath retention — Valsalva risk in cardiac patients- No rapid breathing — minimum 8-second cycles- Exhale ≤ 2x inhale — no evidence for extreme ratios- Immediate exit, always — q or Ctrl+C restores the terminal even on crashThe README includes a resonance frequency measurement protocol for anyone with a chest-strap HRV monitor who wants to find their individual optimum instead of using the 6 bpm default.macOS only (uses afplay for audio cues). MIT licensed.pip install breathe-cliorbrew tap marekkowalczyk/breathe && brew install breathe.

extra.story_text: I built a terminal app that paces slow breathing at 6 breaths per minute for vagal tone training. It's a single Python file, stdlib only, no dependencies — just run breathe and follow the bar.I'm a cardiology patient (HFrEF). Slow breathing at resonance frequency is one of the few non-pharmacological interventions shown to improve cardiac vagal tone and baroreflex sensitivity (Bernardi et al., Circulation 2002; Lancet 1998). I wanted a frictionless daily habit tool — no app store, no account, no subscription, just open terminal and go.Design constraints, all grounded in the clinical literature:- No breath retention — Valsalva risk in cardiac patients- No rapid breathing — minimum 8-second cycles- Exhale ≤ 2x inhale — no evidence for extreme ratios- Immediate exit, always — q or Ctrl+C restores the terminal even on crashThe README includes a resonance frequency measurement protocol for anyone with a chest-strap HRV monitor who wants to find their individual optimum instead of using the 6 bpm default.macOS only (uses afplay for audio cues). MIT licensed.pip install breathe-cliorbrew tap marekkowalczyk/breathe && brew install breathe.

title: Show HN: Jynx, a matchmaking app to find gaming teammates
author: akiro____
body:
TL;DR: Jynx is a gaming social platform that matches you with compatible teammates based on skill level, play style and schedule. Swipe to find players (Tinder-style), create or join game sessions (LFG), chat, and build your squad. 214k lines of Dart, 23 feature modules, built entirely with Claude Code as my entry into agentic engineering.Live on App Store and Play Store:
https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=app.jynx
https://apps.apple.com/fr/app/jynx-where-gaming-gets-social/...---Hi HN, long time lurker, first time poster, be gentle.Developer by day, vibe coder by night: Jynx is the project I used to ease into agentic engineering.AI talks are mitigated, at best. But I'll talk about my experience here. Forgive my erratic style, it is what it is.Working with Claude from the very beginning, it's been a blast. I had the "chance" to have the time necessary to learn and use AI a lot. Lots of different techniques that quickly became completely obsolete today.Without LLMs, it would have been extremely hard to have the same app than I have today. I used Flutter (Dart) to avoid having to dev and maintain two codebases. It is not a language I knew. Learning the language first would have severely hindered the process.For me, from copy/paste to using MCP then Roo Code, then Claude Code was an ecstatic process. I always loved having ideas but the time it would take me to build the thing and test it always felt too long. Not anymore.So we carefully designed, iterated and implemented the two codebases for Jynx. One for the flutter app, one for the firebase backend. I chose Firebase to avoid having to maintain a server and be able to focus on the UI/UX of the app.We started thinking about it in December 2024 and started devs early 2025; not working on it full time at all. We really poured our heart into it and we truly tried to make it as secure as possible. Even though we mean business, it is a passion project. By using the excuse of learning agentic flows, I took the time to inspect each aspects of the app's systems thoroughly.Tech stack:
- Flutter 3.41 / Dart 3.11 (single codebase, iOS + Android)
- Firebase (Firestore, Cloud Functions in TypeScript, Auth, Storage, FCM)
- Riverpod 3.1 + Freezed + json_serializable for state management & immutable models
- Drift for encrypted local SQLite caching (offline-first architecture to optimize Firebase costs)
- Clean Architecture with feature modules and mixin-based repositories
- Sentry + Firebase Crashlytics for production error reporting
- Freerasp for runtime app self-protection (tamper detection, root/jailbreak)Agentic engineering artifacts:
- Claude Code (Claude + GLM) as primary coding agent
- 22 hooks, 18 skills, 13 instincts, 8 rule files, custom subagents, slash commands, MCP servers and plugins (instincts system from Affaan's https://github.com/affaan-m/everything-claude-code)
- GitNexus
- MemPalace for persistent context across sessionsStats: 1,239 Dart files, 214k lines of code (excluding generated boilerplate), 30k lines of comments across the Flutter codebase.I made a detailed cheatsheet document about my whole setup if you want it. I could post it or you DM me.If you have questions, ask away, I'll gladly answer.Test it and tell me what you think of it honestly, I won't get offended!Take care,
Antoine

title: Show HN: Claude-account – switch Claude Code accounts without logging in again
author: hamza_rehman
body:
I use separate Claude Code accounts for work and personal projects. Having to log out and go through the login flow every time I switched accounts became annoying, so I built a small CLI to solve it.The commands are intentionally simple:claude account add myworkaccount
claude account add mypersonalaccount
claude account use myworkaccount
claude account currentAfter switching, Claude Code works normally:claude
claude "fix this bug in main.py"
Repository: https://github.com/hamzarehmandeveloper/claude-accountGive it a try

title: Show HN: TurboGPT: train 22KiB transformer in 13s
author: lostmsu
body:
# lostmsu/TurboGPT

Train a tiny GPT in under a minute (CUDA only)

- Stars: 35
- Forks: 0
- Watchers: 35
- Open issues: 0
- License: MIT License
- Default branch: master
- Created: 2026-09-23T20:21:23Z

## Languages

- C++
- Cuda
- Nix
- PowerShell
- Python

## Top Contributors

- lostmsu (9 contributions)

---

## README

# turboGPT

Tiny byte-level GPT training in CUDA C++. MIT.

## Build

Linux/NixOS:

```bash
nix-build -o build/nix-result
```

Windows, Visual Studio 2022 C++ tools, and CUDA 13.4:

```powershell
.\build.ps1 -CudaArch 86
```

`CudaArch` is the GPU compute capability from NVIDIA's CUDA GPU list.

## Run

```powershell
.\build\turbogpt.exe --data hn1g.txt --log-to runs/ctx4
```

The run stores its checkpoint at
`runs/ctx4/ctx4.pt`, containing model, optimizer, scheduler, and trainer state.
Use `--load CHECKPOINT.pt` to resume it.

`runs/ctx4/report.json` is derived from the log directory. Logs are TensorBoard-compatible:
one report per batch, capped at 8Mi reports, and flushed with periodic or final checkpoints.

## Result

- hn1g after 1.5G training tokens: **2.5295 BPB**.

## Tests

```powershell
python tests\verify.py
```
